The approach employs a recurrent neural network (RNN) to predict the activity of a specific neuron based on the activity of all neurons in the organism. The model's efficacy is evaluated using the correlation coefficient between predicted and actual activity, with results indicating that the proposed method outperforms a baseline model. Furthermore, the model demonstrates the ability to predict the activity of neurons that were not included in the training dataset. Finally, the research explores the potential of this model for inferring synaptic connections between neurons. This study examines the stationary vertex woodland model under a regional constraint, where the vertex set is restricted to a finite region. We demonstrate that the partition function of this constrained model corresponds to the partition function of the unconstrained model but with modified weights. Furthermore, we establish that the constrained model exhibits a phase transition, with the critical point determined by the specific region. Finally, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of the partition function as the region expands to infinity. In this limit, the critical point converges to that of the unconstrained model, and the partition function grows exponentially at a rate equal to the free energy of the unconstrained model. Additionally, we prove that the partition function of the constrained model is always positive. These findings are derived using the transfer matrix method, which is applicable to the vertex woodland model. Consequently, our results extend to the transfer matrix formulation of the six-vertex model. Finally, we outline several open questions for future research. This paper investigates the Gelfand pairs (G, K) where G equals SL(2, p) and K represents a maximal compact subgroup. We demonstrate that for any irreducible representation $\pi$ of G, the space of K-invariant vectors, denoted as $\pi^K$, has a dimension of at most 2. Furthermore, we provide an explicit classification of all irreducible representations $\pi$ for which $\dim \pi^K = 2$. Additionally, we establish that the pair (SL(2, p), D_{2p}) constitutes a Gelfand pair. Finally, we examine the case where p is an odd prime and K is a Borel subgroup, proving that (SL(2, p), K) is a Gelfand pair if and only if p equals 3 or 5. In this specific scenario, we also determine the dimensions of the multiplicity spaces associated with the irreducible representations. The results presented herein are derived from the author's Master's thesis. This study investigates the structural characteristics of crystalline-ice regions within non-crystalline ices, which are hypothesized to exist in the atmospheres of cold gas giant planets. We employed molecular dynamics simulations to generate amorphous solid water (ASW) and hyperquenched glassy water (HGW) models, subsequently analyzing their structures using the pair distribution function (PDF) and radial distribution function (RDF). Our findings indicate that both ASW and HGW contain crystalline-ice regions, with the HGW regions exhibiting a more ordered structure. Furthermore, we observed that the size of these crystalline-ice regions in HGW is significantly larger than in ASW. These results suggest that the formation of crystalline-ice regions in non-crystalline ices is influenced by the initial water structure and the quenching process. Additionally, we propose that the crystalline-ice regions in HGW are more likely to serve as nucleation sites for ice clouds in the atmospheres of cold gas giant planets. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the atmospheres of cold gas giant planets. The source code for the simulations is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1999/ice-cloud. The Earth's magnetosphere is a dynamic system where plasma and magnetic fields interact, generating low-frequency waves that can be detected by ground-based magnetometers. This study explores methods to make these magnetospheric waves audible to the human ear. We introduce a novel technique for rendering these waves perceptible, which involves applying a frequency-dependent gain to the data. This approach is compared against the widely used Hilbert-Huang Transform (HHT) method. Our findings indicate that the gain-based method is more effective at preserving the original waveforms while simultaneously enhancing the signal-to-noise ratio. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method can be easily implemented in real-time. Consequently, we conclude that the gain-based approach is the optimal solution for rendering magnetospheric waves audible. Finally, we provide a web-based application that allows users to listen to magnetospheric waves using this technique. The application is accessible at https://ulf-audio.herokuapp.com/. This study examines the thermodynamic characteristics of ionized, rotating dilaton black membranes interacting with logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics. We derive the metric for these black membranes and analyze their thermodynamic properties, including the first law, entropy, and heat capacity. Furthermore, we investigate the stability of these systems within the canonical ensemble. Our findings indicate that the heat capacity exhibits divergent behavior at specific points, signifying phase transitions. Additionally, we observe that the system's stability is contingent upon the values of the dilaton parameter and the nonlinear electrodynamics coupling constant. Finally, we explore the impact of the nonlinear electrodynamics coupling constant on the system's stability. These results offer valuable insights into the thermodynamic behavior of such black membranes. Photoevaporation and magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) disk wind models offer competing explanations for the observed gas outflows from protoplanetary disks. To differentiate between these mechanisms, we must measure the physical properties of the outflows, specifically their mass-loss rates and the ratio of molecular to atomic gas. This study presents a new analysis of the TW Hydrae (TW Hya) outflow, utilizing a novel model that incorporates both photoevaporation and MHD disk wind components. We applied this model to archival data from the Very Large Array (VLA) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), analyzing the 1.12 GHz and 1.3 cm spectral lines of neutral hydrogen (HI) and molecular hydrogen (H2), respectively. Furthermore, we propose that the HI outflow from TW Hya may be detectable by the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) at 1.12 GHz, offering a unique opportunity to study the photoevaporative wind of TW Hya. Multi-group broadcasting is a critical function in millimeter-wave (mmWave) networks, where a base station (BS) transmits distinct data streams to multiple user groups. To enhance spectral efficiency, hybrid encoding is employed to simultaneously deliver these streams. However, this approach introduces a significant challenge: the BS must identify the optimal hybrid encoding matrix to minimize the total transmission power required for all groups. This paper addresses this issue by proposing a low-complexity hybrid encoding algorithm that utilizes a two-stage optimization process. In the first stage, the problem is decomposed into two sub-problems, which are solved sequentially to determine the optimal hybrid encoding matrix. In the second stage, a low-complexity search algorithm is applied to further refine the matrix. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves a substantial reduction in transmission power compared to existing methods. Additionally, the algorithm exhibits superior performance in terms of both spectral efficiency and computational complexity. Finally, the study confirms that the proposed method is highly effective in mmWave networks characterized by a high density of users. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1998/Hybrid-encoding.

Keywords: mmWave networks, multi-group broadcasting, hybrid encoding, low complexity.

The $r$-process, responsible for creating the majority of heavy elements in the universe, is a complex phenomenon involving rapid neutron capture and beta decay. A critical aspect of this process is the variation in nuclear weights, which significantly influence the resulting elemental abundances. However, the extreme conditions of the $r$-process environment make it impossible to measure these weights experimentally. Consequently, we have developed a machine learning model to predict nuclear weights with the necessary precision for $r$-process studies. This model utilizes a graph neural network, where each node represents a nucleon and edges denote the interactions between them. Our results demonstrate that the model achieves a mean absolute error of 0.0015 atomic mass units (u) for nuclei with mass numbers $A \leq 100$ and 0.0025 u for $A \leq 150$. Furthermore, we show that the model's predictions align with the most recent experimental data. These findings indicate that our approach can accurately predict nuclear weights for the $r$-process, thereby enhancing the precision of $r$-process simulations. Additionally, we provide the model's source code and a user-friendly interface to facilitate its application. This work paves the way for future research into the $r$-process. Sapphire is extensively utilized in quantum technologies, particularly for microwave photonics and superconducting qubits, where its dielectric dissipation is a critical factor. This study presents a precise measurement of sapphire's dielectric dissipation at microwave frequencies, achieving a sensitivity of 10⁻¹⁰. The experimental approach involves a superconducting cavity with a sapphire rod, cooled to 20 mK, and analyzed using a quantum-limited microwave amplifier. The measured dielectric dissipation of 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ aligns with prior literature, while the uncertainty of 10⁻¹⁰ represents an improvement of four orders of magnitude over previous results. Furthermore, the observed temperature dependence of the dielectric dissipation is consistent with established models. These findings offer a precise characterization of sapphire's dielectric properties, which is essential for the advancement of quantum technologies. Additionally, the developed measurement technique is applicable to other materials, enabling the detection of dielectric dissipation at the 10⁻¹⁰ level. This capability is especially valuable for investigating novel materials, such as those with superconducting gaps, where dielectric dissipation is expected to be negligible. The method's sensitivity is limited only by the microwave amplifier's noise temperature, which can be further reduced through the implementation of quantum-limited amplifiers. Ultimately, this research provides a foundation for the development of quantum materials with minimal dielectric dissipation. This study introduces a two-stage resilient optimization framework designed to address uncertainty in both the objective function and decision variables. The model incorporates a first-stage design phase followed by a second-stage operational phase, where the objective is to minimize the worst-case total cost across all scenarios. This reformulation is then resolved using a branch-and-cut algorithm, which integrates two specific cutting planes to tighten the relaxation. Numerical experiments are conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the Lagrangian dual approach effectively handles large-scale instances, and the inclusion of the cutting planes significantly enhances the quality of the lower bounds. Furthermore, the numerical analysis confirms the practical relevance of the model by applying it to a real-world case study. Finally, the study concludes with a discussion of the findings and potential avenues for future research. We introduce a new algorithm for the Set Disjointness problem, where two parties, Alice and Bob, each hold a subset of $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ and must determine if their intersection is empty. Our approach operates within $O(\log n)$ rounds and utilizes $O(n^{1/2+\epsilon})$ bits of communication for any $\epsilon > 0$. This method is straightforward and relies on a novel application of the randomized method of moments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our algorithm can be adapted to the data stream model, enabling two parties to solve Set Disjointness using $O(n^{1/2+\epsilon})$ bits of memory. This result yields a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1/2+\epsilon})$ for the space complexity of any data stream algorithm addressing the distinct elements problem. Additionally, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1/2+\epsilon})$ for the space complexity of any data stream algorithm that approximates the number of distinct elements within a $(1+\epsilon)$-factor. These findings are significant because they represent the first non-trivial lower bounds for these problems in the data stream model. Finally, we show that our algorithm can be extended to the Set Intersection problem, allowing two parties to compute the size of the intersection of their sets using $O(n^{1/2+\epsilon})$ bits of communication. This extension also provides a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1/2+\epsilon})$ for the space complexity of any data stream algorithm solving the distinct elements problem. Our algorithm is conceptually simple and can be implemented using a straightforward random walk. We believe this approach may inspire new techniques for addressing other fundamental problems in communication complexity and data streams. We demonstrate that the platform groups of bicritical rational functions, which are post-critically finite and possess a degree of at least 3, are isomorphic to the symmetric groups of order 3, 4, or 5. MoS$_2$ and WS$_2$ are emerging as promising materials for next-generation electronics, with their electronic properties being a critical factor. This study employs density functional theory (DFT) and GW methods to investigate the work function, ionization potential, and electron affinity of these materials across varying thicknesses. Our findings indicate that the work function of MoS$_2$ and WS$_2$ decreases as thickness diminishes, a trend attributed to the reduction in band gap. Additionally, we observed that the ionization potential and electron affinity of both materials are nearly identical. These results offer valuable insights for the design and fabrication of MoS$_2$ and WS$_2$-based devices. Furthermore, we analyzed the impact of different exchange-correlation functionals on the work function, revealing that the PBE functional yields the most accurate values. Finally, we examined the effects of lattice mismatch and strain on the work function of these materials. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/AbdulRahman123456789/MoS2_WS2. We introduce a novel approach to universal supervised learning, where a delta lens is employed to transmit modifications from a teacher to a student. This method is demonstrated through a simple example involving a teacher and student who share a common input and output, with the student's parameters adjusted to match the teacher's. We prove that this modification transmission is equivalent to a specific type of backpropagation. Furthermore, we extend the framework to scenarios where the teacher and student possess distinct parameters, demonstrating that the delta lens can still facilitate the transfer of the teacher's knowledge to the student. Finally, we outline several potential applications of this lens-based modification transmission. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robinvanlunen/delta-lens. This study examines the uniform constant phase approximation (UCPA) for solutions to the Helmholtz equation, defined by the condition that the phase function $S$ maintains a Lipschitz constant of at most 1. We demonstrate that UCPA solutions can be formulated as solutions to a specific first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equation. Furthermore, we establish the existence of UCPA solutions for a broad class of Helmholtz equations and prove that these solutions are unique within a particular functional space. Finally, we derive an explicit formula for the solution in the case of a constant coefficient. The primary instrument for these findings is a novel first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equation, which we term the constant phase Hamilton-Jacobi equation (CPHJ). We establish the existence and uniqueness of CPHJ solutions in a functional space characterized by restricted smoothness, specifically requiring the gradient to belong to $L^p$ for some $p>1$. This result is achieved through a new viscosity solution framework that accommodates nonconvex Hamiltonians. Additionally, we provide a formula for the solution to the CPHJ equation when the Hamiltonian is convex. These findings are applicable to various wave propagation problems, including the constant phase time approximation, the constant phase time approximation with a source, and the constant phase time approximation with a source and a potential. The CPHJ equation also holds significance in the study of the eikonal equation. Finally, we present numerical simulations to validate our theoretical results. The primary contribution of this work is the formulation of the CPHJ equation, which enables the analysis of UCPA solutions within a space of restricted smoothness. This approach is particularly valuable for wave propagation scenarios involving singularities, such as caustics, where the phase function's gradient is not bounded. The CPHJ equation is also relevant to the eikonal equation. Numerical simulations are included to support these findings. This study investigates the steady-state solutions of rarefied gas flows using the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method. We examine two scenarios: the Couette flow between two parallel plates and the flow around a sphere. Our findings indicate that the DSMC algorithm can reach steady-state conditions within dozens of cycles. Furthermore, we observe that the DSMC solution converges to the steady state with a rate of $O(1/N)$, where $N$ represents the number of particles. These results are validated by comparing the DSMC outcomes with analytical solutions. Finally, we demonstrate that the DSMC solution can be obtained within a few dozen cycles by employing a particle number $N$ that is 10 to 100 times greater than the minimum required for the DSMC algorithm. This approach significantly reduces the computational cost of DSMC simulations. Consequently, we conclude that DSMC is a viable method for simulating rarefied gas flows. This paper introduces the concept of stiff fibrations and establishes their connection to precise fibrations. We demonstrate that every stiff fibration possesses a precise cover, and conversely, every precise fibration can be realized as a stiff fibration through a specific construction. Furthermore, we prove that the class of stiff fibrations is closed under pullbacks, covering projections, and countable compositions. Finally, we provide a characterization of countable compositions of stiff fibrations using the notion of a weakly precise fibration. Additionally, we examine the relationship between precise fibrations and precise spans, showing that a fibration is precise if and only if its associated fibration of precise spans is also precise. Finally, we establish that the class of precise fibrations is closed under covering projections and countable compositions. The paper concludes with an example of a precise fibration that is not a stiff fibration.

Subsequently, it presents three primary ZNN models tailored for time-varying matrix problems: the Constant Time-Varying ZNN (CTZNN) model, the Exponential Time-Varying ZNN (ETZNN) model, and the Finite-Time Time-Varying ZNN (FTZNN) model. The paper then details the application of these models to forecasting computations, covering both time-invariant and time-varying scenarios. Finally, it outlines future research directions for ZNNs in the context of forecasting computations. The primary objective of this work is to provide a comprehensive overview of ZNNs for solving time-varying matrix challenges, specifically within forecasting computations. The proposed models are designed to be simple, efficient, and highly accurate. This study introduces a new deep learning architecture designed for image classification, featuring a multi-scale, multi-stream framework. The system comprises two parallel streams: one utilizing a convolutional neural network (CNN) and the other employing a multi-scale convolutional neural network (MSCNN). These streams are integrated via a novel on-off center-surround (OCS) mechanism, which functions as a dynamic fusion strategy. The OCS module adaptively selects the optimal stream for each image based on its specific characteristics. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed OCS network surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, the model exhibits robustness against adversarial attacks, maintaining high classification accuracy even when images are perturbed. X-ray optics are essential for focusing and imaging in the 0.1–10 keV range, yet their performance is often constrained by the inherent limitations of refractive and diffractive designs. This paper reviews recent advancements in X-ray optical technologies aimed at broadening the field of view and improving image quality. We examine the impact of various aberrations, including astigmatism, field curvature, and distortion, and discuss methods to mitigate them through precise alignment, the use of aspheric surfaces, and optimized detector placement. Additionally, we address the challenges of manufacturing and testing high-quality X-ray optics, highlighting the critical role of metrology in ensuring the necessary surface accuracy. Finally, we present examples of successful X-ray imaging systems that have achieved wide fields of view and high spatial resolution. These developments are expected to significantly advance X-ray astronomy and microscopy. The paper concludes with a discussion of future directions for X-ray optical technology. We demonstrate that the magnetic Bloch theorem applies to twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, provided the field strength is quantized at $2\pi$ flux per moiré unit cell. This theorem enables the construction of the TBG Hamiltonian using a magnetic Bloch basis, revealing that the system's spectrum consists of a series of flat bands. Furthermore, we show that these flat bands exhibit a reentrant behavior, meaning they vanish and reappear as the magnetic field varies. This phenomenon is attributed to the nontrivial topology of the Bloch bundle. Our findings offer a theoretical framework for interpreting recent experimental results regarding the $2\pi$ flux state in TBG. Additionally, we propose that the $2\pi$ flux state can be interpreted as a superposition of two distinct phases: a ferromagnetic phase and a quantum anomalous Hall phase. Finally, we suggest that the $2\pi$ flux state may serve as a platform for investigating the interplay between ferromagnetism and superconductivity. These insights could facilitate the design of novel quantum materials and devices. The accompanying Python code is available at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/TBG_2pi_flux. Steganography involves concealing secret messages within innocuous-looking media, such as embedding text inside images. While prior research has primarily focused on image-based steganography, this study explores the creation of steganographic content using text. We introduce a novel steganographic system that embeds secret messages into innocuous text generated by a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network. Our approach employs a two-stage process: first, an LSTM model is trained to produce text that mimics a specific author's style; second, a genetic algorithm is utilized to embed the secret message within the model's output. We evaluated our method on two datasets, the Enron email dataset and the IMDB movie review dataset. The results demonstrate that our system successfully embeds secret messages into innocuous text while maintaining the stylistic characteristics of the original author. Furthermore, we show that the embedded text remains coherent and that the secret message can be reliably extracted. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the system's performance. Unit commitment (UC) is a critical challenge in power system operations, involving the determination of optimal generator statuses and power outputs to satisfy demand while minimizing costs. Although numerous methods exist for solving UC, they often struggle with scalability and real-time performance. This paper introduces a novel approach to accelerate UC solutions by employing a machine learning model to estimate the expense of specific unit commitment constraints. This learning-based expense model is integrated into the UC formulation to reduce the number of constraints evaluated during the solution process. The proposed method is validated using a 10-generator system, demonstrating its effectiveness in solving UC problems. Results indicate that the method can achieve up to a 50% reduction in constraint evaluation time. Furthermore, the study confirms that the machine learning model maintains high accuracy even when trained on a limited dataset. Finally, the paper discusses the method's limitations and potential avenues for future research. The Kitaev model, which describes a quantum spin liquid in a honeycomb lattice, has been a subject of intense study. This work reports the first experimental observation of the breakdown of antiferromagnetic order in the Kitaev material $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ under uniaxial stress. We demonstrate that the magnetic structure transitions from a dimerized state to a collinear antiferromagnetic configuration, a change that can be explained by a stress-induced shift in the Kitaev coupling. Furthermore, we show that the stress-induced dimerization is driven by the competition between the Kitaev coupling and the Heisenberg exchange interaction. These findings offer new insights into the nature of the quantum spin liquid state in Kitaev materials. Additionally, we discuss the potential for tuning the Kitaev coupling in other Kitaev compounds, such as $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$, through applied stress. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for the search for a quantum spin liquid state in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$. Synthetic control methods are widely used to estimate causal effects, yet their theoretical underpinnings remain unclear. This paper introduces a new framework for synthetic controls that offers a more robust theoretical basis for causal inference. We demonstrate that the method's validity relies on two key assumptions: (1) the treated unit is a linear combination of donor units, and (2) the weights assigned to donor units are non-negative. We provide a theoretical analysis of the method's properties and propose a novel approach for estimating causal effects. Furthermore, we develop a statistical test to evaluate the validity of the synthetic control method. Finally, we apply this framework to estimate the causal impact of the 1995 Colombian peace accord on the electoral outcomes of the FARC party. Our findings indicate that the FARC's vote share increased by 10.5% following the agreement. Additionally, we show that the synthetic control method yields more accurate estimates compared to difference-in-differences. This paper introduces a novel distributed algorithm for computing the Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) divergence between two graphs. The proposed method is designed to operate in a distributed setting, where each graph is partitioned into subgraphs, and the GW divergence is calculated locally for each pair of subgraphs. To ensure security, we employ a local differential privacy (LDP) mechanism to safeguard the privacy of each graph during the computation. We demonstrate that the resulting algorithm is both distributed and private, and we provide theoretical analysis of its convergence and error bounds. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to validate the algorithm's performance. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/GW-DSP.

We introduce a novel laser-plasma electron injection mechanism driven by the self-steepening of an intense circularly polarized laser pulse. This self-steepening effect generates a strong, ultra-short, and intense electric field at the pulse's trailing edge, which facilitates electron injection. The resulting electron bunch exhibits high energy, a compact size, and a short duration. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this injected electron bunch can be boosted to ultra-relativistic energies through a single pass through a plasma wakefield. This self-steepening injection method offers a promising pathway for achieving high-quality electron beams. Additionally, we show that the self-steepening effect can be significantly enhanced by employing a linearly polarized laser pulse. This approach enables the generation of high-energy, high-quality electron beams using a single laser pulse, thereby reducing the complexity of the experimental setup. Finally, we confirm that the boosted electron beams possess high charge, high energy, and a small transverse size. These findings suggest that self-steepening injection could serve as a viable alternative to traditional injection techniques. Our results provide a new method for generating high-quality electron beams and open new avenues for laser-plasma acceleration research. Furthermore, this study offers a novel perspective on the self-steepening effect, which is crucial for advancing ultrafast laser technology. The proposed self-steepening injection technique is expected to have broad applications in fields such as particle physics, medical imaging, and material science. This study examines the generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov framework, which encompasses the standard $n$-dimensional case as a specific instance. We derive the most general form of the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian for this system, subsequently identifying all Lie point symmetries and the associated Noether point symmetries. Furthermore, we establish the general conditions required for the existence of a first integral within the framework. Finally, we apply these findings to the standard $n$-dimensional Ermakov system. The results demonstrate that the standard $n$-dimensional Ermakov system possesses a significantly higher degree of symmetry compared to the generalized version. Additionally, we show that the standard $n$-dimensional Ermakov system is superintegrable when $n=2$ and $n=3$. Finally, we provide a general method for constructing the general solution of the standard $n$-dimensional Ermakov system. The transport feed serves as a critical component of the German news ecosystem, yet its digital format remains inaccessible to individuals with print disabilities. This study introduces a neural network architecture designed to generate the transport feed from a newspaper's masthead. The model utilizes a recurrent neural network to process the masthead sequentially, employing a self-attention mechanism to capture long-range dependencies. Additionally, a novel loss function is implemented to enhance the model's ability to handle the feed's inherent structure. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms a baseline model. Furthermore, the system's output is evaluated by human readers, confirming its practical utility. This method is straightforward to implement and can be integrated into existing few-shot learning frameworks. This result is demonstrated through the specific example of a non-relativistic charged scalar field. Furthermore, we provide a counterexample to illustrate that the non-reversibility condition is essential. Finally, we discuss the implications of this theorem for the Higgs mechanism. The proof relies on the continuity equation, the Gauss law, and the commutation relations between the charge and the field. Consequently, this derivation does not require Lorentz invariance, the existence of a mass gap, or the presence of a vacuum state. Additionally, we examine the theorem's validity in the context of the Schwinger model. The findings presented here are intended to complement the analysis found in the review by Weinberg. The tau lepton is a fundamental particle with a mass of 1.777 GeV/c² that decays into hadrons. Identifying these hadronic tau decays is a critical component of the physics analysis at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This study introduces a deep neural network designed to distinguish hadronic tau decays from other particles, specifically jets and leptons. The network was trained using simulated data from the CMS experiment at the LHC. The results demonstrate that the proposed deep neural network achieves performance comparable to the standard CMS tau identification algorithm. Furthermore, the network's ability to identify hadronic tau decays is validated through its application to the search for the Higgs boson decaying into a tau lepton pair. The analysis indicates that the deep neural network can enhance the sensitivity of this search. Additionally, the paper provides a detailed description of the network's architecture and training methodology. Finally, the source code for the deep neural network is made available to the public. The abundance of data from astronomical surveys like the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST) and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory (VRO) presents a significant challenge for data analysis. While deep learning has proven effective for classification tasks, it often struggles with uncertainty quantification. This study introduces a Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) approach to address this limitation. We trained a BNN on the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) galaxy dataset to classify galaxies into elliptical, spiral, and irregular categories. Our results demonstrate that the BNN achieves classification accuracy comparable to that of a standard neural network. Furthermore, the BNN successfully quantifies uncertainty, identifying misclassified galaxies with high confidence. This capability is particularly valuable for future data analysis, as it allows for the targeted collection of additional data to refine the classification of uncertain objects. Consequently, this method offers a promising pathway for analyzing the extensive datasets expected from upcoming surveys. We present a theoretical analysis of intermodal Brillouin scattering within solid-core photonic crystal threads. This study examines the interplay between the Brillouin gain spectrum and the frequency separation between the fundamental and first-order modes. Our findings indicate that the first-order mode can be excited via intermodal scattering, resulting in a narrow Brillouin gain spectrum. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the frequency spacing between the fundamental and first-order modes can be tuned by adjusting the core diameter. These results suggest that photonic crystal threads are promising candidates for implementing narrow-band Brillouin amplifiers and filters. Additionally, we explore the potential for intermodal Brillouin scattering to facilitate the excitation of higher-order modes in these waveguides. Finally, we outline the experimental requirements necessary to observe this phenomenon. The proposed intermodal Brillouin scattering mechanism may also be applicable to other photonic waveguides. This study addresses two combinatorial optimization problems: the Set-Union Rucksack Problem (SURP) and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem (BMCP). In both scenarios, a decision-maker must select a subset of items from a given collection to maximize the coverage of a universe of elements, subject to a budget constraint. The objective is to identify the optimal subset that covers the maximum number of elements. We introduce a novel local search algorithm that integrates a new neighborhood structure with a specialized data structure to enhance both the efficiency and effectiveness of the search process. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods on SURP and BMCP instances. Furthermore, we show that our method can be readily adapted to solve other related problems. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/rodrigo-fernandez/ls-surp. Attrition forecasting is a critical component of business analytics, particularly for online games where player retention directly impacts revenue. This study introduces a new forecasting method that models the attrition process as a sequence of independent Bernoulli trials, with the probability of a successful trial determined by a logistic function of time. The model's parameters are estimated using the method of moments, and its performance is evaluated through simulation and a real-world case study. The results demonstrate that the proposed model is both accurate and computationally efficient. Furthermore, the paper examines the relationship between attrition and player spending, offering insights into how attrition models can inform revenue forecasting. Finally, the study concludes by outlining potential future research directions. The source code for the model is accessible at https://github.com/robertk1990/attrition-forecasting.

We introduce a new framework for deriving gluon transverse-momentum-dependent parton distributions (TMDs) from high-momentum effective theory. This approach offers a systematic method to calculate gluon TMDs within the light-front gauge, which is essential for interpreting them as Wilson-line-averaged light-front wave functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that gluon TMDs can be extracted from the gluon field strength tensor. Finally, we apply this formalism to compute the gluon TMDs for the pion and proton at leading order. These results align with previous calculations in the light-front gauge and confirm that gluon TMDs are non-zero at leading order. Additionally, we observe that gluon TMDs for the pion and proton exhibit distinct behaviors, particularly in the small-$x$ region. Our findings indicate that gluon TMDs for the pion are significantly larger than those for the proton, a conclusion supported by recent experimental data. This suggests that gluon TMDs may play a crucial role in explaining the observed nuclear modification of pion production in high-energy proton-nucleus collisions. Furthermore, our results suggest that gluon TMDs could be a key factor in explaining the unexpectedly large elliptic flow of pions in heavy-ion collisions. These insights may also offer a new perspective on the origin of the chiral magnetic effect. Finally, we note that our results are consistent with those obtained using the axial gauge. Ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions serve as a unique environment for investigating the interaction between electrons and positrons and dense nuclei. This study examines the electromagnetic interaction of low transverse momentum electrons and positrons with lead nuclei during ultra-peripheral collisions. We demonstrate that the cross-section for the photoproduction of electron-positron pairs by a lead nucleus is approximately $10^4$ times greater than that for proton-antiproton pairs. Furthermore, we show that the cross-section for the photoproduction of electron-positron pairs by a lead nucleus is roughly $10^5$ times larger than the cross-section for the photoproduction of muon-antimuon pairs. These findings indicate that electron-positron pairs are the most probable electromagnetic products of ultra-peripheral ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Additionally, we present the cross-sections for the photoproduction of electron-positron pairs by lead nuclei as a function of the electron-positron pair invariant mass and the electron-positron pair rapidity. We also calculate the total number of electron-positron pairs produced in ultra-peripheral ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Finally, we discuss the potential for detecting electron-positron pairs in ultra-peripheral ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. These results may be valuable for future research in this field. This study examines a nonlocal model of traffic congestion, where vehicle density is represented by a function $u$ defined on the interval $[0,1]$. The model incorporates a nonlocal interaction term, $J*u$, with $J$ being a smooth, nonnegative kernel that is normalized to integrate to 1. The evolution of $u$ is governed by the equation $u_t = (u(1-u-u(0)J*u))_x$, subject to the boundary condition $u_x(0,t) = u(1,t)$. We demonstrate that this equation admits a unique entropy solution. Furthermore, we analyze the singular limit as the kernel $J$ approaches a Dirac mass, showing that the resulting limit equation possesses a unique entropy solution. Finally, we establish the convergence of the nonlocal model's entropy solution to that of the limit model. We demonstrate that the critical dynamics of a generic dilation surface are characterized by a collection of saddle links situated on its horizons, which are defined as invariant tori. Furthermore, we establish that the critical dynamics of a generic dilation surface constitute a dilation analogue to the well-known theory of Morse-Smale vector fields on three-dimensional manifolds. Finally, we outline the dilation surface's counterpart to the Poincaré return map, which is a piecewise affine map acting on a two-dimensional manifold. These findings are anticipated to facilitate the classification of generic dilation surfaces. Additionally, we provide a dilation surface analogue to the Poincaré-Bendixson theorem, which asserts that the critical dynamics of a generic vector field on a two-dimensional manifold are either periodic or chaotic. This result is particularly significant for understanding the critical dynamics of Teichmüller flows on moduli spaces of surfaces of genus two or higher. We also present a dilation surface analogue to the Smale horseshoe, which serves as a paradigm for chaotic dynamics. Finally, we illustrate the application of these results to the Teichmüller flow on the moduli space of genus two surfaces. Specifically, we show that the critical dynamics of a generic Teichmüller curve are either periodic or chaotic, and that the critical dynamics of a generic Teichmüller flow on the moduli space of genus two surfaces are either periodic, chaotic, or possess saddle links on their horizons. These findings are expected to be applicable to the study of Teichmüller flows on moduli spaces of surfaces of genus three or higher. We introduce a functional network model of the human brain that incorporates all 86 billion neurons and 100 trillion synapses, utilizing a complete correlation matrix. This model is constructed by integrating the anatomical structure of the brain with the functional architecture of the human mind. We demonstrate that the network's eigenvalues and eigenvectors can be analytically derived from the correlation matrix. Furthermore, we show that the network's stability is governed by the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix, which are determined by the eigenvectors of the Laplacian matrix. Finally, we establish that the human brain functions as a critical network. These findings offer a novel perspective on the brain's structure and dynamics, with potential applications in neuroscience, neurology, and psychology. Additionally, this work provides a foundation for developing a new type of brain-computer interface. This paper introduces a novel unitary transformation, the Clifford algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann (C-S-B) map, which extends the standard Segal-Bargmann transformation. We demonstrate that this map is equivalent to the Taylor isomorphism, establishing a link between the Hilbert space of square-integrable holomorphic functions and the Fock space of square-integrable functions on phase space. Furthermore, we show that the C-S-B map maps the harmonic oscillator Hamiltonian to the Laplacian on the complex plane. Finally, we provide an explicit formula for the C-S-B map and outline its applications in quantum mechanics. These findings are anticipated to be valuable for researchers in both mathematics and physics. The results were achieved through the application of the coherent state method. Additionally, we present a new proof of the Bargmann-Fock theorem, which is also expected to be of interest to the scientific community. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the coherent state method and the Segal-Bargmann transformation; Section 3 introduces the C-S-B map and proves its equivalence to the Taylor isomorphism; Section 4 applies the C-S-B map to the harmonic oscillator; and Section 5 offers a new proof of the Bargmann-Fock theorem. The paper concludes with a discussion of the results.

The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is a next-generation neutrino observatory designed to investigate the fundamental properties of neutrinos and their role in the universe. By utilizing a high-intensity proton beam to generate a massive flux of neutrinos, DUNE will conduct a comprehensive analysis of the three neutrino flavors. The experiment will employ a 40-kiloton liquid argon time projection chamber situated 1,300 kilometers underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota, with a near detector located at Fermilab. This setup will enable the precise measurement of neutrino oscillation parameters, including the CP-violating phase, thereby advancing our understanding of the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the cosmos. Additionally, DUNE will significantly enhance our knowledge of supernova dynamics, solar physics, and geophysics. This paper outlines the scientific objectives of DUNE and the technological innovations required to achieve them. The project is currently in its final design phase, with construction anticipated to begin in 2020. The DUNE collaboration comprises over 1,000 scientists and engineers from 30 nations. In reinforcement learning, experience replay is a widely adopted technique for improving sample efficiency. This paper introduces a novel experience replay strategy designed to enhance policy performance. The proposed method, Variance Decrease based Experience Replay (V-DEER), aims to minimize the variance of the value function estimates used to update the policy. We demonstrate that the variance of these estimates is directly proportional to the number of samples collected during the replay process. Consequently, we develop a sampling algorithm that prioritizes data points with lower variance. Experimental results on both continuous and discrete control tasks indicate that V-DEER significantly outperforms existing experience replay methods. Furthermore, we show that V-DEER can be seamlessly integrated with various reinforcement learning algorithms. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/V-DEER. Rust's type system is renowned for guaranteeing memory safety without requiring runtime checks. However, this approach often restricts the expressiveness of Rust programs, particularly when dealing with dynamically sized types. This paper introduces Josephine, a new language that extends Rust by incorporating a novel mechanism for managing the lifetimes of dynamically sized types. Josephine is designed to be a superset of Rust, allowing it to be compiled into Rust code. We present the language's syntax and semantics, demonstrate its utility through examples, and outline the compilation process. Furthermore, we provide a formal proof showing that Josephine code compiles to Rust code that is memory safe. Finally, we discuss the implementation of the compiler and its integration with the Rust compiler. The language is named after Josephine Butler, a 19th-century British feminist and social reformer who advocated for women's rights. This study introduces a polar subcode technique for list decoding belief propagation (BP) channels. The method involves polarizing the channel to isolate a polar subcode capable of supporting a specific target list size. We demonstrate that the polar subcode's capacity approaches the channel capacity as the block length increases. Furthermore, we establish that the polar subcode maintains a constant rank distance, ensuring a minimum distance that does not diminish with block length. Leveraging these properties, we develop a polar subcode-based list BP decoder that achieves list decoding with a target size of $2^L$ for any $L \geq 1$. Additionally, we prove that the average number of decoding iterations required by this list BP decoder remains constant regardless of the block length. This paper introduces a method for creating a combined PSF that is both accurate and computationally efficient. The approach involves convolving the two PSFs, which are first aligned and then resampled to a common grid. The resulting combined PSF is highly accurate, with a maximum error of approximately 0.0001. Furthermore, the algorithm is efficient, requiring only a few seconds to convolve two PSFs with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 1 arcsec. This efficiency is achieved by limiting the number of PSF pixels to a maximum of 100, which is sufficient for most applications. The method is implemented in the Python package `psfcombine`, which is available at https://github.com/roelofsm/psfcombine. The package includes a function to generate a combined PSF from two input PSFs, as well as functions to align and resample PSFs to a common grid. Additionally, the package provides a function to create a PSF from a Moffat model, which is useful for testing the accuracy of the combined PSF. This study introduces a new method for modeling biological cell shapes using implicit neural representations. We demonstrate that these representations can be effectively trained on shape data from the CellShapes dataset, which comprises 2D contours of 1,000 cells from the yeast *S. cerevisiae*. Our approach utilizes a neural network to learn a continuous, differentiable function that maps 2D points to real values, where the zero-level set delineates the cell boundary. The network is trained via a loss function that minimizes the discrepancy between the predicted zero-level set and the actual cell contours. We show that the resulting implicit representation is capable of generating new cell shapes and that these generated shapes exhibit statistical properties comparable to those of real cells. Furthermore, we highlight the potential of this method for applications in cell shape analysis and simulation. The code is accessible at https://github.com/robertkroger/implicit-cell-shapes.

Keywords: implicit neural representations, generative modeling, cell shape analysis, cell shape simulation.

We introduce XLNet, a pretraining approach designed to enhance language comprehension. Unlike BERT, which utilizes a masked language modeling objective, XLNet employs an autoregressive pretraining method that leverages the autoregressive nature of language generation. This strategy enables XLNet to capture both causal and bidirectional dependencies within the input. Additionally, XLNet incorporates a universal pretraining objective that integrates various auxiliary tasks, such as next token prediction, to boost performance on downstream tasks. Empirical results demonstrate that XLNet surpasses BERT on numerous benchmarks, including GLUE, SQuAD, and RACE. Furthermore, XLNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on several tasks where BERT had previously failed, such as the CMRC 2016 and DuReader passage reading comprehension challenges. We conducted a detailed analysis of the impact of stellar activity on the transmission spectra of the hot Jupiter HD 209458b, utilizing both low- and high-resolution data. Our findings indicate that stellar activity affects both spectral resolutions similarly, with the primary distinction being that high-resolution spectra allow for the identification of specific activity features. Consequently, we conclude that high-resolution observations do not solve the issue of stellar contamination. Instead, they offer a means to identify and characterize the activity, enabling researchers to determine the extent of its influence on the data. This approach is particularly valuable for low-resolution transit spectroscopy, where the presence of stellar activity can be confirmed. Ultimately, we argue that high-resolution data serves as a complementary tool for low-resolution observations, facilitating the characterization of stellar activity and the assessment of its impact on exoplanet atmospheric studies. This synergy is especially critical for future missions like the James Webb Space Telescope, which will rely on low-resolution instruments. Centipedes are renowned for their exceptional swimming capabilities, yet the specific mechanisms enabling their rapid and agile movement remain unclear. This study investigates the swimming kinematics of the centipede *Scutigerella immaculata* using high-speed video recordings. We observed that the animal's body bends significantly during locomotion, with the head and tail exhibiting opposite bending directions. Furthermore, the swimming speed of *S. immaculata* is directly proportional to the magnitude of this body bending. These findings suggest that the centipede's agility is achieved through a unique swimming strategy that differs from the conventional undulatory motion seen in other aquatic animals. Additionally, we developed a simple mechanical model to explain the observed dynamics, which successfully accounts for the experimental data. This model indicates that the centipede's swimming performance is primarily driven by the interaction between its body and the water interface. Overall, our results provide new insights into the swimming mechanics of centipedes and highlight the critical role of the water interface in their locomotion. These findings may also offer inspiration for the design of bio-inspired swimming robots. This study presents a flexible simulation of tsunami propagation following an asteroid impact. The methodology involves a two-stage process: first, a high-resolution finite element model generates the initial wave field, and second, a low-resolution finite difference model simulates the subsequent propagation. The initial wave field is derived from a 100-meter asteroid striking the ocean at 20 km/s. The resulting wave field is analyzed using a Fourier transform to determine the dominant frequency and wavelength. Furthermore, the wave height is calculated at the coast of the Iberian Peninsula. These findings are compared against results from a similar asteroid impact in the Pacific Ocean. The research concludes that the proposed method is effective for simulating tsunamis generated by asteroid impacts. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the Fourier transform serves as a valuable tool for characterizing the wave field, while the finite difference model accurately replicates the wave height observed in the Pacific Ocean. Finally, the study suggests that this approach could be applied to investigate the potential for asteroid impacts to generate tsunamis in the Mediterranean Sea. We present JWST/NIRCam and NIRSpec observations of a sample of 12 optically faint, infrared-luminous galaxies (L_IR > 10^11 L_sun) at redshifts of 0.5 < z < 1.5, which were previously identified as optically dim in the COSMOS-Web survey. These galaxies exhibit a median stellar mass of 10^10.5 M_sun and a median star formation rate of 1.5 M_sun/yr. Our analysis reveals that their star formation is primarily driven by a compact, central starburst component, with a median size of 0.5 kpc. The specific star formation rates of these galaxies are comparable to those of star-forming galaxies at similar redshifts and stellar masses. Furthermore, we find that the star formation rates of these optically dim galaxies are significantly lower than those of their optically bright counterparts at the same redshift and stellar mass. This discrepancy is attributed to the optically bright galaxies hosting a more extended star-forming component, which is absent in the optically dim group. Consequently, optically dim galaxies represent a distinct population characterized by a central starburst and a lack of extended star formation. This study marks the first detection of the physical properties of optically dim galaxies using JWST data. The COSMOS-Web survey will provide a larger sample of these galaxies, enabling a more robust statistical analysis of their characteristics. Additionally, the optically dim population is expected to be a significant contributor to the total star formation rate density at z > 1.5. Finally, we demonstrate that optically dim galaxies are likely to be detected by JWST, even when they are optically faint. This study examines the impact of external electric fields on the interaction energies of 110 molecular dimers from the S66 benchmark set. The dimers, which are primarily non-covalent, were modeled using the CCSD(T)/aug-cc-pVQZ method. The analysis reveals that the electric field induces a non-linear response in interaction energy, with the magnitude of this effect varying across different dimers. Furthermore, the field alters the equilibrium geometry of the dimers, resulting in shifts in both interaction energy and its components. The most significant changes in interaction energy occur in dimers featuring a single hydrogen bond, where the electric field can either strengthen or weaken the interaction. Additionally, the field modifies the relative contributions of various energy components, such as electrostatics, dispersion, and exchange-repulsion. Finally, the study demonstrates that the electric field can induce a transition between two distinct dimers. These findings are crucial for understanding how external fields influence molecular dimers in biological systems and other environments. This paper introduces a robustness metric for cyber-physical systems (CPS) grounded in Signal Temporal Logic (STL). We demonstrate that the robustness degree of a CPS trajectory relative to an STL formula can be computed by integrating the robustness degree of the underlying signal with the robustness degree of the control input. Furthermore, we establish that this metric adheres to the standard properties of robustness, including monotonicity, additivity, and boundedness. Finally, we illustrate the application of this metric through a case study involving a quadrotor. The source code for the metric is accessible at https://github.com/ahmed-ahmed10/STL-Robustness.

This paper introduces a new category of probabilistic automata called Abstract Concealed Markov Models (ACMMs). ACMMs extend Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) by incorporating a non-deterministic, potentially infinite, internal state that remains concealed from the outside. This internal state is modeled as a monad, which is a standard mathematical structure for representing computational effects. We demonstrate that the behavior of an ACMM can be described as a Kleisli category, where the Kleisli arrows represent the observable behavior of the model. Furthermore, we provide a quantitative analysis of ACMMs, showing that their behavior can be represented as a metric space. Finally, we apply this framework to analyze data flow in a simple programming language. In this application, the internal state of an ACMM represents the program's memory, while the concealed state represents the program's control flow. We illustrate how this approach can be used to measure the data flow between two programs. The paper concludes with a discussion of the framework's limitations and potential future research directions. This paper introduces a privacy metric for location tracking that relies on the conditional expectation of a user's position. We demonstrate that this metric adheres to the standard axioms of privacy measures and establish a connection between it and the privacy level of a corresponding anonymized dataset. Furthermore, we examine the trade-off between privacy and utility, proving that the privacy-utility trade-off curve is concave. Finally, we propose a method for generating synthetic data that achieves any specific point on this curve. The effectiveness of our approach is validated through experiments using real-world taxi trajectory data. Additionally, we outline a future research direction aimed at developing a privacy metric based on conditional entropy. This paper introduces a novel 3D localization framework utilizing the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation. The system comprises two primary components: a lightweight NDT encoder and a Transformer-based decoder. The encoder efficiently compresses 3D point clouds into a compact NDT representation, while the decoder employs a Transformer architecture to perform localization by integrating the NDT encoding with a learned prior map. The decoder is trained end-to-end using a large-scale dataset of 3D point clouds paired with ground-truth poses. Extensive experiments on the KITTI and nuScenes datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in 3D localization. Furthermore, the model exhibits strong generalization capabilities, successfully adapting to unseen environments. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) connectivity is a widely used method for investigating brain function and structure. However, the reliability of rs-fMRI findings remains uncertain due to the inherent noise in the data. This study introduces a statistical framework to evaluate the robustness of rs-fMRI results, specifically focusing on the stability of connectivity strength and the accuracy of predicting brain function. These findings offer a robust statistical basis for interpreting rs-fMRI connectivity and its relationship with brain function. Beeping networks consist of wireless nodes that can only detect the presence of a signal without identifying its source. This paper introduces a new algorithm for constructing a naming scheme in such networks, where each node is assigned a unique name from a predefined set. The scheme must ensure that every node can eventually determine its own name. We demonstrate that our method requires a naming set of size $O(n^2)$, where $n$ represents the total number of nodes. This result improves upon the previously best-known algorithm, which utilized a naming set of size $O(n^3)$. Furthermore, we establish that our algorithm is optimal up to a constant factor by proving that any naming scheme for beeping networks must employ a set of at least $\Omega(n^2)$ names. Additionally, we present a randomized algorithm that achieves a naming set size of $O(n \log n)$ with high probability. Finally, we examine the scenario where nodes lack knowledge of the network size and propose a naming scheme that functions correctly regardless of $n$. In this context, we show that our algorithm is optimal up to a constant factor, requiring a naming set of size $O(n)$, and we also provide a lower bound of $\Omega(n)$ for this specific case. The performance of our algorithms is evaluated through simulations. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robertk1999/Beeping-Networks. Transformer-based models have achieved remarkable success in natural language processing, yet they struggle with code-mixed languages due to a lack of positional encoding. This paper introduces PESTO, a novel dynamic and relative positional representation designed to address this gap. Experimental results demonstrate that PESTO significantly enhances the performance of various Transformer models on code-mixed datasets. The isotope effect on the critical temperature ($T_c$) in H$_3$S hydride superconductors is investigated using the Eliashberg theory, with pressure serving as a variable. Our findings indicate that the isotope influence on $T_c$ is highly sensitive to pressure. Specifically, at a pressure of 150 GPa, the isotope effect coefficient $\alpha$ is approximately 0.5, whereas it rises to 0.7 at 200 GPa. This variation is attributed to the proximity of the Fermi level to the van Hove singularity. Furthermore, we observe that the isotope effect on $T_c$ diminishes as the pressure increases. These results are consistent with experimental data. Additionally, we demonstrate that the Eliashberg theory accurately predicts the isotope effect on $T_c$ for H$_3$S hydride superconductors. Finally, we conclude that the Eliashberg theory is applicable to other superconductors, including MgB$_2$, LaH$_{10}$, and LaH$_{11}$. This study provides a theoretical basis for understanding the isotope effect in H$_3$S hydride superconductors. Motion planning for robots operating in dynamic environments is a critical challenge. This paper introduces a new method for generating motion plans that account for the movement of obstacles. The proposed approach constructs a graph where nodes represent the robot's possible positions, and edges denote feasible transitions between them. The graph is built by identifying a set of key points and connecting them with feasible paths. To ensure the resulting graph remains connected, the method employs a novel technique for creating spatial restrictions. This process involves defining a set of candidate points and selecting the optimal subset to guarantee connectivity. The paper provides a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's computational complexity and demonstrates its effectiveness through various examples. Finally, the method is applied to a real-world scenario involving a mobile robot navigating a warehouse. The results indicate that the proposed approach successfully generates motion plans for the robot. Furthermore, the method is shown to be adaptable for use in other applications. Visual relocalization is a critical component of many robotic systems, including autonomous vehicles and drones. This paper introduces a new visual relocalization method that integrates learned features with a surfel map. The approach employs a lightweight, efficient, and robust feature extractor to generate features from both the current camera frame and the map. A learned feature matcher is then utilized to align the current frame's features with those stored in the map. To enhance the accuracy of the initial pose estimate, a pose graph optimization is performed using the matched features. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and computational efficiency. We demonstrate that the logical function semifield of a tropical curve is finitely generated over the tropical semifield. This result is achieved by establishing a correspondence between logical functions and specific rational functions defined on a finite set of points within the tropical curve. Furthermore, we provide an algorithm to determine a finite generating set for any given logical function semifield. As a consequence, we prove that the logical function semifield of a tropical curve is isomorphic to a logical function semifield of a tropical hypersurface. Additionally, we derive a criterion for deciding whether a logical function is constant. Finally, we present an algorithm to compute a finite generating set for the logical function semifield of a tropical hypersurface. These findings are applied to investigate the algebraic properties of logical functions and their semifields. Specifically, we examine the relationship between the algebraic structure of a logical function semifield and the geometric structure of its corresponding tropical hypersurface, and we provide a criterion for determining when a logical function semifield is finite. Finally, we establish a criterion for identifying when a logical function semifield is isomorphic to a polynomial semifield over the tropical semifield. These results are illustrated with examples. The paper concludes with several open questions. We conducted a detailed study of the nematic instability in the iron-based superconductor LiFeAs using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Our results indicate that the Fermi surface remains intact across the entire temperature range, from above the superconducting transition temperature down to the lowest measured temperatures. This observation contradicts the hypothesis that nematicity drives the superconducting state in LiFeAs. Furthermore, we detected a significant suppression of the superconducting gap below the superconducting transition temperature, which is consistent with the coexistence of superconductivity and nematicity. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the pairing mechanism in LiFeAs. This study examines the global fit of the Type-II two-Higgs-doublet model (2HDM) in light of anticipated results from the LHC and future colliders. We analyze the impact of projected measurements for the Higgs boson mass, the top quark mass, and the W boson mass, alongside the potential discovery of the light CP-odd scalar ($A$) and the light CP-even scalar ($h_2$). Our findings indicate that the 2HDM parameter space is significantly constrained by these future measurements, with the most stringent limits arising from the W boson mass. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the 2HDM can be distinguished from the Standard Model through a combination of Higgs boson coupling measurements and the discovery of the $A$ and $h_2$ states. Finally, we illustrate that the 2HDM can be probed at future colliders even if the $A$ and $h_2$ particles remain undetected. These results underscore the critical role of future colliders in advancing our understanding of the 2HDM. The analysis was conducted using the HiggsTools software package. The complete code and associated data are accessible at https://github.com/2HDMfit/2HDMfit. Experimental results indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods in both accuracy and efficiency. This paper introduces a damped inertial dynamics framework designed to solve the minimization of a convex, lower semicontinuous function $f$ over a Hilbert space, with a focus on converging to the minimum norm solution. The system incorporates a Tikhonov regularization term with a time-varying coefficient that vanishes asymptotically, alongside a viscous damping term and a regularized gradient of $f$. We demonstrate that this dynamics is well-posed and establish its asymptotic convergence toward the minimum norm minimizer. Furthermore, we derive a convergence rate for the regularized objective function values and prove that the trajectories converge weakly to the minimum norm solution. Finally, numerical experiments are provided to validate the theoretical findings. These results extend the work of Attouch, Cabot, and Peypouquet (2019), who addressed the same problem using a constant Tikhonov regularization coefficient. Additionally, our approach offers a robust alternative to the inertial proximal algorithm proposed by Chambolle and Pock (2011) for finding the minimum norm solution. The proposed dynamics can be interpreted as a continuous-time formulation of a Nesterov-type algorithm. Finally, we show that the trajectories of this dynamics are bounded in energy and exhibit asymptotic regularity. These properties are essential for analyzing the asymptotic behavior of the trajectories and establishing the convergence rate of the regularized objective values. The proof of the convergence rate relies on a novel application of the Lojasiewicz inequality. This work is a joint effort with the authors of Attouch, Cabot, and Peypouquet (2019). The primary distinction between the two approaches lies in the time-varying nature of the Tikhonov regularization coefficient in our method, which ensures convergence to the minimum norm solution. In contrast, Attouch, Cabot, and Peypouquet (2019) utilized a constant coefficient, resulting in convergence to a generic minimizer. Consequently, our method is particularly advantageous when the minimum norm solution is required. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the problem formulation and the proposed dynamics; Section 3 establishes the well-posedness of the dynamics; Section 4 proves the asymptotic convergence of trajectories to the minimum norm solution; Section 5 derives the convergence rate for the regularized objective values; and Section 6 presents numerical experiments to illustrate the theoretical results. The proofs of asymptotic convergence and the convergence rate are detailed in Appendices A and B, respectively.

This study examines the stability of a wheeled robot with a fixed wheelbase that adheres to a vertical surface. The robot's wheels are powered by two motors, and its body is connected to the wheels via two springs and dampers. The wheelbase is assumed to be sufficiently long to generate a normal force on the wall through the robot's body dynamics. The system is modeled as a hybrid dynamical system, where the continuous dynamics are governed by a differential equation and the discrete dynamics by a reset map. The differential equation is derived using the method of virtual work, while the reset map is formulated based on the robot's contact with the wall. The study analyzes the stability of the system's equilibria and periodic orbits, demonstrating that the robot can exhibit both stable and unstable behaviors. Furthermore, it is shown that the robot's dynamics can be controlled by adjusting the spring and damper parameters. Finally, numerical simulations are provided to illustrate the robot's behavior. The paper concludes with a discussion of the results and potential future research directions. The study is intended for researchers and engineers working on robot design and control. It is also accessible to students and professionals interested in robotics and control theory. The paper is written in a clear and concise style, making it easy to understand for readers with a basic background in mathematics and physics. The authors hope this work will inspire further research into the design and control of robots capable of adhering to vertical surfaces. The paper is also available in Spanish. We investigate the impact of extended impurities on the microwave conductivity of kinetic energy-driven superconductors, specifically focusing on the two-dimensional dirty limit. Our analysis reveals that the microwave conductivity exhibits a strong dependence on the energy gap, a factor that is particularly significant in the context of cuprate superconductors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the microwave conductivity is highly sensitive to the specific shape of the energy gap. Finally, we establish that the microwave conductivity of a superconductor with extended impurities can be accurately described by the Drude model. These findings are derived from a rigorous analytical treatment of the kinetic energy-driven superconductor's response to an external electromagnetic field. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive discussion of the physical mechanisms underlying these results. Our study offers a detailed examination of the microwave conductivity in kinetic energy-driven superconductors, with a specific emphasis on the effects of extended impurities. We anticipate that these results will prove valuable for interpreting experimental data regarding the microwave conductivity of cuprate superconductors. Finally, we believe our findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of the physics governing kinetic energy-driven superconductors. The results indicate that GrowSpace is both usable and effective, with participants expressing interest in applying it to other plants. We present a rigorous derivation of the Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) cycle by conformally gluing quantum disks. This approach yields a novel construction of the SLE cycle that is distinct from the established method of conformally gluing quantum cones. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the resulting SLE cycle exhibits the same scaling limit as the one derived from conformally gluing quantum spheres. Finally, we establish that the SLE cycle generated through quantum disk gluing possesses the property of conformal invariance. These findings are achieved by employing the quantum gravity formalism developed in \cite{DG2020} and utilizing the results from \cite{DG2021}. Additionally, we provide a new proof of the scaling limit for the SLE cycle arising from conformally gluing quantum spheres, which relies on the quantum gravity formalism and the findings of \cite{DG2021}. This proof is notably more concise than the original argument presented in \cite{DG2020}. The primary innovation of this work lies in the application of the quantum gravity formalism to rigorously derive the SLE cycle via conformally gluing quantum disks. We anticipate that this methodology will facilitate the derivation of other scaling limits for random surfaces. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 offers a brief overview of the quantum gravity formalism; Section 3 reviews the scaling limit of the SLE cycle from conformally gluing quantum spheres; Section 4 introduces the scaling limit of the SLE cycle from conformally gluing quantum disks; and Section 5 provides a rigorous derivation of this scaling limit. We propose that the primordial black hole (PBH) responsible for the gamma-ray burst GRB 090510 originated from a collapsing region of enhanced curvature. This scenario is viable because the oscillating curvaton, which drives inflation, generates a power spectrum with a sharp peak at the horizon scale. Consequently, the resulting PBHs exhibit a narrow mass distribution centered on the horizon scale. Furthermore, the curvaton's oscillations can produce a large curvature perturbation, leading to the formation of PBHs with masses approximately $10^{10}$ times the horizon scale. This mechanism offers a potential explanation for the existence of supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies. Additionally, we demonstrate that the PBHs formed in this way can account for the observed gamma-ray burst GRB 090510. Finally, we show that the curvaton model can simultaneously explain the observed baryon asymmetry of the universe. These findings suggest that the curvaton model is a promising framework for understanding the early universe.
