We present a theoretical investigation of a time-reversal-violated Weyl semimetal within the Hofstadter regime, where the Hofstadter butterfly spectrum emerges from the superposition of the lattice Brillouin zone and magnetic Brillouin zone. In this regime, the Weyl points are no longer isolated but instead form continuous lines. We demonstrate that these lines can be categorized into two distinct types: those that are closed and those that are open. Furthermore, we show that the Chern number associated with the open lines is non-zero, whereas the Chern number for the closed lines is zero. Finally, we propose a method to detect these Weyl lines using the anomalous Hall effect. This study offers a novel perspective on Weyl semimetals under strong magnetic fields and provides a new framework for investigating topological phases in this domain. Additionally, it suggests a potential experimental approach for identifying Weyl lines through the anomalous Hall effect. The findings are supported by numerical simulations. We introduce a hybrid dielectric-plasmonic nanoantenna designed to generate a highly luminous, unidirectional light source. This device consists of a dielectric nanoparticle positioned above a metallic film, with a plasmonic nanorod placed between them. The dielectric nanoparticle functions as a Mie resonator, while the plasmonic nanorod acts as a dipole antenna. By adjusting the nanorod's length, we can control the phase of the dipole's oscillation to achieve constructive interference with the Mie resonator's dipolar mode. This interference results in a strong, unidirectional emission. Furthermore, the plasmonic nanorod enhances the local electromagnetic field, thereby increasing the overall luminosity of the source. We demonstrate that this hybrid nanoantenna can be excited by a laser beam and serve as an efficient, unidirectional light source. Additionally, we show that the system can be tuned to emit at specific wavelengths, such as 633 nm, by varying the dimensions of the nanorod. This research holds significant potential for applications in nanophotonics, including nanoscale optical tweezers, nanoscale optical microscopy, and nanoscale optical communication. This study investigates the electronic properties of silicene supported on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) when decorated with manganese (Mn) atoms. We examine various adsorption configurations, including top, bridge, and hollow sites, as well as different orientations of the Mn atoms. Our findings indicate that the Mn atoms preferentially occupy the hollow sites of the hBN substrate. Furthermore, the Mn atoms induce a significant opening of the band gap in the silicene layer, transforming it from a semimetal into a semiconductor. Additionally, the Mn atoms generate a magnetic moment within the silicene system. These results suggest that Mn-decorated silicene could serve as a promising candidate for spintronic applications. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the electronic and magnetic characteristics of the Mn-decorated silicene/hBN system. Sgr A East, a radio source located near the Galactic center, is hypothesized to be the remnant of a stellar explosion that occurred approximately 200 years ago. This study investigates the explosion's origin by analyzing the source's morphology and the distribution of its radio emission. We propose that the explosion site was situated roughly 0.1 pc from the Galactic center, a location that aligns with the observed radio emission. Furthermore, we suggest that the explosion was driven by a stellar wind with a mass-loss rate of approximately 10^-4 solar masses per year. Finally, we conclude that the explosion site was likely a massive star, potentially a Wolf-Rayet star, rather than a black hole. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that Sgr A East is a stellar-mass supernova remnant. This study examines the production of two Higgs bosons in association with a vector boson at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) using the ATLAS detector. We introduce a digital alkaline spin maser that utilizes a single spin qubit to generate a coherent microwave field. This device operates by employing a quantum non-demolition measurement to extract information regarding the spin state, thereby inducing a back-action that drives the maser. Furthermore, we show that the maser can be controlled to emit a single photon into a specific mode of a microwave cavity. The proposed technology is compatible with existing solid-state spin qubits, such as those found in diamond and silicon carbide. Additionally, we outline a potential implementation using a superconducting qubit as the maser pump. This proposal is experimentally feasible, as it leverages the established ability to couple superconducting qubits to microwave cavities and to control their spin states via nuclear spins. We anticipate that this work will inspire further research into maser-based quantum technologies. The accompanying paper provides a detailed experimental proposal for the digital alkaline spin maser. This paper introduces a randomized Newton approach for distributed convex optimization, where each agent possesses a local convex objective function and communicates with neighbors via a connected network. The proposed algorithm operates in two stages: first, agents collaboratively compute a global Newton direction using only local information, and second, they perform a line search along this direction. We demonstrate that the algorithm achieves global convergence and establish a worst-case iteration complexity of $O(1/\epsilon)$ to reach an $\epsilon$-stationary point. Furthermore, we prove that the method converges to an $\epsilon$-stationary point in $O(\log(1/\epsilon))$ iterations when the objective functions are strongly convex. Finally, numerical experiments are provided to validate the algorithm's performance. These results indicate that the proposed method is highly effective for distributed convex optimization, particularly when the objective functions are strongly convex. Additionally, the algorithm exhibits robustness against communication delays and packet losses, maintaining performance even under such constraints. We examine the temporal dynamics of a system of $N$ particles evolving under a stochastic process, where the time scale of interest is defined by the mean first passage time (MFPT) to a target set. We demonstrate that the MFPT scales as $N^2$ when the target set is small, but transitions to a linear dependence on $N$ when the set is large. This shift in scaling behavior occurs at a critical set size, $N_c$, which is determined by the system's geometry and the specific stochastic process. We provide an analytical estimate for $N_c$ and validate it through numerical simulations. Furthermore, we show that this transition is linked to the emergence of a non-trivial stationary distribution for the particle system. Finally, we apply these findings to a model of a polymer chain diffusing in a solvent, where the target set represents a specific conformation. In this context, the transition from quadratic to linear scaling in the MFPT is driven by the competition between the polymer's self-avoidance and the solvent's confinement. Our results indicate that the MFPT scales quadratically with $N$ when the solvent is large, but becomes linear when the solvent size approaches $N_c$, a value that increases with the polymer's self-avoidance. We also discuss the implications of these findings for the design of DNA-based nanomachines. The paper concludes with a discussion of the broader significance of these results. This study introduces a new approach for calculating the complicated scaling factor (CSF) of the static electric polarizability of atoms and molecules under strong direct current (DC) fields. The method relies on the linear response function of the ground state, which is derived using the time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) framework. By employing the outside-in scheme, the CSF is determined through the integration of the linear response function. The accuracy of this proposed method is validated by comparing its results for the CSF of the hydrogen atom and the hydrogen molecule against those obtained from the conventional inside-out scheme. Furthermore, the method's performance is evaluated for the hydrogen molecule across various interatomic distances. Finally, the study examines the CSF for the hydrogen molecule under strong DC fields, analyzing its dependence on both the field strength and the interatomic distance. The findings indicate that the outside-in scheme yields accurate results for the CSF of the hydrogen molecule under strong DC fields. Additionally, the CSF exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with the interatomic distance, reaching a minimum at approximately 3.0 Bohr. This behavior is attributed to the significant cancellation between the direct and exchange components of the exchange-correlation kernel. These results suggest that the outside-in scheme is a viable and efficient method for computing the CSF of atoms and molecules in strong DC fields. The research also highlights the potential for further applications of this approach to other atoms and molecules. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the algorithm's logarithmic variant and provide a characterization of the resulting limit. This study presents the first measurement of the top quark pair production cross-section in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV, utilizing the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis incorporates 13.6 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected during the 2017 run. The measured cross-section is $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 820 \pm 10 \pm 10$ pb, where the uncertainties correspond to statistical and systematic errors, respectively. This result aligns with Standard Model predictions and is consistent with measurements taken at the higher energy of 13 TeV. Additionally, the differential cross-sections for the $p_T$ and rapidity of the top quark, as well as the $p_T$ of the top quark pair, are reported. These differential distributions are compared against various theoretical models, including those derived from next-to-next-to-leading order QCD calculations. The observed data generally agree with the theoretical predictions. Furthermore, the measured cross-sections are compared with those obtained at 13 TeV to investigate the energy dependence of the $t\bar{t}$ production process. The findings are consistent with theoretical expectations, which predict a 10% increase in the total cross-section and a corresponding rise in the $p_T$ and rapidity distributions as the collision energy rises from 5.02 to 13 TeV. Finally, the $p_T$ distribution of the top quark is compared with predictions from the POWHEG+PYTHIA8 and POWHEG+HERACLES Monte Carlo event generators. Both models accurately describe the measured data, with POWHEG+HERACLES providing a slightly better fit. The analysis also examines the impact of varying the renormalization and factorization scales on the predicted cross-sections. The POWHEG+HERACLES model demonstrates a smaller scale dependence than POWHEG+PYTHIA8, indicating that the former is more robust against uncertainties in these parameters. This suggests that POWHEG+HERACLES is a more reliable tool for predicting $t\bar{t}$ production cross-sections at the LHC. The study concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for future LHC physics. The results are consistent with Standard Model predictions and provide valuable insights into the $t\bar{t}$ production mechanism at the LHC. This paper introduces a novel class of analytic functions defined via generalized Bessel functions, which extends the class introduced by Janowski. This study evaluates the performance of nonlinear field-separated preconditioners for two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media. We compare the standard Schur complement preconditioner with two novel variants: the field-separated Schur complement preconditioner and the field-separated additive Schwarz preconditioner. Numerical experiments demonstrate that these new preconditioners achieve superior convergence rates compared to the standard Schur complement approach. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of varying permeability contrasts and grid sizes on preconditioner performance. Finally, we examine the effects of different nonlinear solvers and time-stepping schemes on the overall solution process. The results indicate that the field-separated preconditioners are highly effective for two-phase flow simulations in heterogeneous porous media. The study examines the propagation of ideal fluids within a warped spacetime framework, incorporating the cosmological constant. The analysis identifies two distinct families of solutions: one where the fluid's four-velocity aligns with the Killing vector, and another where it is orthogonal. In both scenarios, the fluid's four-velocity is irrotational. Furthermore, the investigation demonstrates that the fluid's four-velocity is geodesic in the first case and shear-free in the second. The paper concludes by presenting the explicit forms of the solutions for both families. Finally, the study explores the physical implications of these solutions, specifically regarding the possibility of warp travel. The results indicate that warp travel is feasible only when the fluid's four-velocity is aligned with the Killing vector, and this is possible exclusively if the fluid is irrotational. Additionally, the study shows that the fluid's energy density must be negative, and the cosmological constant must be positive and sufficiently large to enable warp travel. The geospatial domain is experiencing a surge in data generation, driven by the widespread adoption of IoT devices and the increasing availability of open data. This influx of data is anticipated to significantly influence urban planning and management. Furthermore, it is designed to be extensible, allowing for the addition of new data types and resolutions. The paper also outlines the implementation of this model within a data warehouse environment. Finally, the study demonstrates the model's utility through a case study focused on the city of Turin. We introduce a method to investigate the temperature, motion state distributions, and heating rates of a two-dimensional ion crystal. This approach utilizes the spin decay of a single, optically trapped, and laser-cooled $^{40}\mathrm{Ca}^{+}$ ion embedded within the lattice. By analyzing the spin decay of this central ion, we can determine the temperature of the entire lattice. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the ion's spin decay rate is sensitive to the temperature of the surrounding ions, the distribution of their motion states, and the speed at which the lattice is heated. This technique offers a straightforward and efficient means to characterize the thermal and dynamical properties of trapped ion crystals. We validate this method by measuring the temperature of a 2D $^{40}\mathrm{Ca}^{+}$ lattice and observing how the spin decay rate of the central ion varies with the heating speed of the surrounding ions. Additionally, we show that the spin decay rate of the central ion can be modulated by adjusting the laser intensity of the spin-dependent optical lattice. These findings establish a foundation for developing a new tool to study the thermal and dynamical characteristics of trapped ion crystals. Our results are significant for advancing the study of quantum simulation and many-body physics using trapped ions. This study introduces a fully quantum mechanical approach to investigate the impact of chemical and electromagnetic effects on tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS). The method employs a quantum mechanical model for the tip and a classical model for the substrate, utilizing a quantum-corrected model (QCM) to account for the electromagnetic field. By applying the first Born approximation, the electromagnetic influence is calculated, while the chemical effect is determined through the modification of the tip's polarizability. The resulting enhancement factors are compared against experimental data to validate the model's accuracy. Furthermore, the study examines the influence of the tip's radius and the distance between the tip and substrate on the enhancement factor. Finally, the research explores the potential of this method for analyzing the vibrational modes of single molecules. The findings indicate that the proposed quantum mechanical framework offers a reliable and efficient means to investigate the chemical and electromagnetic effects within TERS. This approach can be extended to other tip-enhanced spectroscopy techniques, such as tip-enhanced Raman scattering (TERS) and tip-enhanced infrared spectroscopy (TEIRS). We conducted a survey of 10 nearby galaxies to detect anomalous microwave emission (AME) and free-free radiation using the Sardinia Radio Telescope (SRT). The SRT's 16-meter dish, equipped with a 1.5 GHz bandwidth, was utilized to observe the K-band (21.5–23.0 GHz) of these targets. Our sample includes the nearby dwarf irregular galaxy NGC 6822, the nearby dwarf spiral IC 10, and eight galaxies from the M81 group. We measured the spectral index ($\alpha$) for each source, where $\alpha$ is defined by $S_\nu \propto \nu^\alpha$. The results indicate that the spectral index for AME is approximately -1.0, while free-free emission exhibits an index of +2.0. We also determined the total flux density for each galaxy. The spectral index for NGC 6822 was found to be -0.9, consistent with prior studies. For the M81 group galaxies, we observed a range of spectral indices from -0.9 to +0.2, with NGC 3079 showing the highest value. The free-free spectral index for NGC 6822 was measured at +2.0, whereas the index for IC 10 was determined to be +1.5. These findings suggest that the emission from NGC 6822 is dominated by AME, while the emission from IC 10 is primarily free-free. The M81 group galaxies display a mix of both emission types. Finally, we calculated the ratio of free-free to AME flux density for each source. The lowest ratio was observed in NGC 6822, while the highest was found in NGC 3079. This study provides the first measurements of spectral indices for AME and free-free emission in the M81 group galaxies. Additionally, we present the first free-free spectral index measurement for IC 10 and the first AME spectral index measurement for NGC 3079. These results will aid in understanding the physical mechanisms driving AME and free-free emission in these galaxies. Furthermore, the data will facilitate future studies of the physical properties of the interstellar medium in these systems. The entropy change associated with the molecular caloric and ferroelectric transition in ammonium sulfate was investigated using inelastic neutron scattering. This study reveals that the transition involves a substantial alteration in the vibrational entropy of the ammonium ion, a finding that contradicts the conventional view of molecular caloric materials, which typically attribute their entropy changes to the orientational disordering of the ammonium ion. Furthermore, the observed entropy change aligns with the transition's classification as a second-order phase transition. These results indicate that ammonium sulfate possesses a unique combination of properties, making it a promising candidate for molecular caloric applications. Additionally, the study demonstrates that inelastic neutron scattering is a highly effective method for determining the entropy change of molecular caloric materials. Finally, the findings suggest that the ammonium ion's orientational degrees of freedom are not essential for molecular caloric behavior. Reinforcement learning (RL) models are frequently employed to analyze how the brain processes reward and punishment. However, the specific computational strategies the brain utilizes to learn from these outcomes remain unclear. This study investigates whether the midbrain's response to prediction errors can reveal the underlying learning mechanisms. We demonstrate that the midbrain's reaction to prediction errors aligns with a suboptimal RL model that incorporates a forgetting factor, rather than an optimal model that does not. Furthermore, we show that the midbrain's response to reward prediction errors is more closely linked to the difference between expected and actual rewards than to the actual reward itself. These findings suggest that the midbrain encodes prediction errors using a suboptimal RL algorithm that includes a forgetting factor. Additionally, we propose that the midbrain's response to reward prediction errors reflects the magnitude of the reward difference, indicating that the midbrain may encode the value of rewards. These results offer new insights into the computational processes of the midbrain and its role in learning from rewards and punishments. This study addresses the problem of identifying the closest neighbor for a query sequence within a database of time sequences, using the Fréchet distance as the metric. We introduce a novel algorithm that achieves a running time of $O(n^2\log n + m\cdot n)$ for a query of length $m$ against a database of length $n$. This performance surpasses the previous best result of $O(n^2\log n + m\cdot n^2)$ established by Buchin et al. (2017). Furthermore, we demonstrate that this runtime is nearly optimal by proving a lower bound of $\Omega(m\cdot n)$ for any algorithm solving this task. Additionally, we extend our approach to the more general scenario of approximate close neighbor searching, where the goal is to find a neighbor within a specified distance threshold. In this context, we show that our algorithm's running time can be reduced to $O(n^2\log n + m\cdot n\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon})$, where $\varepsilon$ represents the approximation factor. Finally, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(m\cdot n\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon})$ for this approximate version, indicating that our algorithm is almost optimal. These findings are derived from a reduction from the element uniqueness problem. Our results are applicable to various domains, including shape matching, motion planning, and bioinformatics. This paper introduces a two-dimensional Z-array code set designed for two-dimensional radar systems. The two-dimensional Z-array is constructed by combining a one-dimensional supplementary code set with a two-dimensional array code set. The one-dimensional supplementary code set is generated using multivariable functions, while the two-dimensional array code set is formed by arranging one-dimensional array codes into a two-dimensional structure. The resulting two-dimensional Z-array code set exhibits low cross-correlation and low auto-correlation properties. Simulation results demonstrate that the two-dimensional Z-array code set is suitable for two-dimensional radar systems. Furthermore, the two-dimensional Z-array code set can be extended to higher dimensions, making it applicable for multi-dimensional radar systems. This work provides a theoretical foundation for the development of multi-dimensional radar systems. Additionally, the two-dimensional Z-array code set offers a reference for the design of two-dimensional radar systems. Finally, the two-dimensional Z-array code set can be utilized in two-dimensional radar systems to enhance the system's performance. The two-dimensional Z-array code set is expected to contribute to the advancement of two-dimensional radar systems. This paper introduces a non-convex variational framework designed to simultaneously reconstruct polyenergetic X-ray CT data, suppress sensor noise, and determine material composition. The approach models the unknown material distribution as a linear combination of basis functions, where the coefficients represent the mass fractions of distinct materials. To address noise, the framework employs a data fidelity term that accounts for Poisson noise. For material decomposition, it utilizes a non-convex total variation (TV) regularization term, which is more effective than convex alternatives at preserving sharp edges. Finally, the CT reconstruction is achieved by minimizing the sum of the data fidelity and TV regularization terms. The study provides a theoretical analysis of the proposed model and its associated optimization algorithm, demonstrating that the algorithm converges to a stationary point. Numerical experiments are included to validate the method's efficacy. The results indicate that the proposed approach successfully reconstructs CT images, reduces noise, and accurately identifies material composition. Furthermore, the method demonstrates superior performance compared to existing techniques in terms of reconstruction quality, noise reduction, and material decomposition accuracy. By employing the hydrodynamic model, we derive the dispersion relation for these modes. These findings are expected to be valuable for the development of new electronic and optoelectronic devices. Digital health records (DHRs) are increasingly utilized to enhance patient care and support clinical decision-making. However, extracting actionable insights from these records remains a significant challenge. While recent advancements in deep learning have enabled the modeling of complex temporal dependencies in DHRs, current approaches often fail to capture the intricate relationships between different data types, such as vital signs and laboratory results. To address this limitation, we introduce the Diverse Similarity Graph Neural Network (DSGNN), a novel framework designed to learn diverse similarity graphs from heterogeneous DHRs. This method constructs a graph where nodes represent individual data points and edges signify their similarities. By integrating these graphs into a graph neural network, the model can effectively capture the interdependencies among various data types. We evaluated DSGNN on a real-world dataset comprising 1,000 patients with sepsis, demonstrating its ability to identify critical features and generate accurate predictions. The results indicate that DSGNN surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in both feature selection and prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the model exhibits robustness against missing data and noise, highlighting its potential for practical clinical applications. This study examines the electric double layer (EDL) at a charged soft interface within an electrolyte solution, incorporating solvent polarization effects. Software specifications are essential for developing high-quality software, yet they are often difficult to create due to the time and effort required. While various approaches exist to derive specifications from existing software, they typically depend on structured source code or documentation. This paper introduces a method for extracting software specifications from unstructured text, such as informal notes, emails, and meeting minutes. The approach involves three main steps: first, identifying and extracting sentences that describe software requirements; second, parsing these sentences to generate a structured representation of the requirements; and third, utilizing the structured data to produce a software specification. We have implemented this method in a tool called SpecGen, which automatically generates specifications from unorganized texts. We evaluated SpecGen using a dataset of 1,000 documents from the Eclipse IDE project, demonstrating that it can automatically create specifications for open-source projects. The results indicate that SpecGen successfully generates specifications for most projects, with the generated specifications being of high quality. Furthermore, we show that these specifications can be effectively used to identify bugs in the projects. By automatically converting these texts into specifications, developers can more easily understand project requirements and contribute to the development process. This study introduces a collaborative network encoding framework designed to enhance energy efficiency in wireless networks. Within this system, relays are strategically scheduled to transmit data to the destination, while power is allocated to maximize the sum-rate. The resulting optimization problem is formulated as a mixed-integer non-linear program (MINLP). To address this, we propose a low-complexity algorithm that jointly optimizes relay timetabling and power distribution. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves a 10% improvement in energy efficiency compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the algorithm's computational complexity is analyzed, and its performance is validated through simulations. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the findings. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/ENC.

High-intensity X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy is a powerful technique for investigating the electronic and structural characteristics of matter. However, the non-linear response of matter to intense X-ray fields complicates the interpretation of experimental data. This study introduces a rate framework to model the time evolution of electron groups within the XANES region. By solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for a two-level system, we derive an analytical expression for the rate of electron group evolution. This approach is validated against numerical simulations and experimental results. The proposed framework offers a novel perspective on the non-linear dynamics of XANES spectroscopy and provides a foundation for interpreting experimental data. Furthermore, it can be extended to more complex systems, such as multi-level systems and those involving multiple electrons. Segmenting MS lesions in MRI scans is a critical step for analyzing disease progression and treatment efficacy. However, variations in imaging protocols across different scanners and sites can significantly impact segmentation performance. This study evaluates the impact of such domain shifts on the segmentation of MS lesions in T2-weighted FLAIR images. We compare two strategies: (1) training a model on a single site and testing it on others, and (2) training a model on multiple sites simultaneously. Our results indicate that while the second approach yields superior performance, it is not always feasible due to the high cost of acquiring data from multiple sources. To address this, we propose a novel method for continual learning that trains a model on a single site while retaining knowledge from previous sites. We demonstrate that this continual learning approach can achieve performance comparable to training on multiple sites simultaneously. Furthermore, we show that this method can be extended to handle multiple domain shifts. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the challenges associated with domain shifts in MS lesion segmentation. This paper introduces a model error structure designed to enhance the machine intelligence of model error within dynamical systems. The proposed structure is defined by two key properties: (i) the model error is represented as a linear combination of a set of basis functions, and (ii) the coefficients for these basis functions are determined through a machine learning algorithm. The study examines the conditions under which this structure can be applied to dynamical systems and demonstrates its effectiveness using a simple example. Furthermore, the paper outlines several potential applications, including the identification of nonlinear systems, the design of nonlinear observers, and the development of nonlinear controllers. Finally, the authors suggest that this model error structure could serve as a foundation for future research into machine intelligence for dynamical systems.

We present new ALMA observations of the Dragon infrared dark nebula, revealing a dense core with a mass of approximately 1000 solar masses and a radius of roughly 0.2 parsecs. The core's density profile follows a power law with an index of -1.5, indicating a flatter structure than previously documented. This profile suggests that the core is expanding inward, a process that may facilitate the formation of massive stars. Additionally, we identified a compact, dense region within the core that could serve as the birthplace of a massive star. This study marks the first detection of a dense core within Dragon, a massive molecular cloud. Our findings support the hypothesis that core expansion is a viable mechanism for triggering massive star formation. Furthermore, the presence of a dense core in Dragon implies that the cloud is in a late evolutionary stage, potentially nearing the end of its star-forming activity. Finally, we observed a significant increase in the dust mass of Dragon, which may be attributed to the formation of a massive star. These results offer valuable insights into the mechanisms driving massive star formation. The data presented in this study are accessible via the ALMA archive. Primordial black holes (PBHs) are hypothesized to have formed in the early universe due to the gravitational collapse of density fluctuations. If PBHs constitute a significant portion of dark matter, their gravitational influence on nearby stars could create a distinctive stellar signature. This study presents PopSyCLE simulations of globular clusters containing PBHs, which reveal a unique stellar distribution characterized by a central depression and an outer ring. We demonstrate that the resulting stellar density profiles can be accurately modeled using a simple analytic function. Furthermore, we show that the stellar density profiles of PopSyCLE simulations featuring both PBH and stellar mass loss are well-described by a single analytic function. Finally, we establish that the stellar density profiles from simulations with both mass loss and PBHs are consistent with those from simulations containing only stellar mass loss. These findings indicate that the stellar density profiles of globular clusters can be effectively modeled using a single analytic function, regardless of whether the underlying physics involves PBHs or stellar mass loss. Consequently, the stellar density profiles of globular clusters cannot be used to constrain the fraction of dark matter composed of PBHs. Additionally, we find that the stellar density profiles of globular clusters are not sensitive to the initial PBH mass function. We present findings from a Monte Carlo simulation of a two-dimensional system consisting of rigid, thin wedges with varying splay angles. The simulation results indicate that the system undergoes a first-order phase transition from an isotropic state to a nematic state. Furthermore, the nematic phase exhibits a sequence of first-order transitions between different stages characterized by distinct splay variations. The calculated free energies for these stages align with the predictions of the Frank-Oseen elastic theory. Additionally, we observe that the free energy of the system is highly sensitive to the distribution of splay angles. Finally, we demonstrate that the system can be modeled as a collection of rigid, wedge-shaped cells. The elastic properties of these cells are derived from the free energy of the corresponding isotropic system. We also examine the implications of these findings for the formation of liquid crystals within biological cells. Specifically, we show that the distribution of splay angles in the wedge-shaped cells of a biological cell can be inferred from the observed splay variations in the resulting liquid crystal. This approach offers a potential method for investigating the internal structure of biological cells. The study concludes with a discussion of the broader implications of these results. While current PEFT techniques typically adjust only a small subset of parameters, they often fail to fully capture task-specific nuances. To address this, we introduce a novel PEFT approach that uniquely adapts a single token to represent task-specific information. Our method, Unique Token Adaptation (UTA), is straightforward to implement and can be seamlessly integrated into existing PEFT frameworks. This paper introduces a novel, non-axiomatic approach to preference ordering for set augmentation problems, where an agent must select a set of items from a menu to maximize their utility. We demonstrate that this method is both computationally efficient and capable of generating a preference ordering that is both non-axiomatic and contextual. Furthermore, we establish that this approach is the sole method that can produce such an ordering. Finally, we illustrate the method's application in a real-world scenario involving the selection of a group of friends for a party. We investigate the thermodynamic and dynamic characteristics of a polymer melt, specifically polyethylene glycol (PEG), across a broad temperature range. Transformer language architectures have recently achieved remarkable success in natural language processing. However, their training and inference processes are computationally intensive, making it difficult to train models on large-scale datasets. To address this, we introduce a novel method for reducing the computational cost of training Transformer models. Furthermore, we show that our approach can significantly lower computational costs while maintaining performance comparable to standard training methods. Finally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the method's effectiveness and its implications for the broader field of Transformer language architectures. Neural Machine Interpretation (NMI) involves translating natural language sentences into executable code. While current NMI models typically generate code token by token, this approach often results in syntactically valid but semantically incorrect programs. To address this, we introduce a look-ahead focus mechanism that directs the model's attention to future tokens during generation. This method is integrated into a novel beam search algorithm that leverages the model's focus to select the most promising code paths. Our results demonstrate that this look-ahead focus strategy significantly enhances the accuracy of the generated code. Additionally, we show that the model's attention mechanism effectively captures the program's control flow. We have made our code and models publicly available at https://github.com/robinson1127/look-ahead-focus. Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have achieved remarkable success in computer vision, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. This paper introduces a novel approach to visualizing the latent representations of these networks. By leveraging the inherent structure of filters, we propose a new visualization technique that highlights the most significant filters within each layer. This method is grounded in the observation that filters in a specific layer are highly correlated with those in the subsequent layer. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on the CIFAR-10 dataset, showing that it effectively reveals the visual semantics of the network's latent representations. Furthermore, we establish a strong correlation between the visual semantics of the final layer and the class labels of the input images. These findings offer valuable insights into the internal workings of DCNNs and pave the way for future research into their latent visual-semantic representations. We introduce a novel phonon-mediated interaction between one-dimensional (1D) cuprates, which is attractive at long ranges and repulsive at short distances. We demonstrate that this interaction can stabilize a CDW state characterized by a period of $2\pi/3$ within a one-dimensional Hubbard model featuring a phonon-mediated attractive potential. This study investigates the impact of turbulent effects on mean-field dynamo models, focusing on the generation of large-scale magnetic fields within convective regions. We introduce a mean-field framework that incorporates both the turbulent magnetic field and the turbulent velocity field. Our findings indicate that the turbulent magnetic field exerts a significant influence on the dynamo process, a conclusion supported by numerical simulations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the turbulent magnetic field can be modeled as a random field with a Gaussian distribution. The implications of these findings for astrophysical phenomena are also discussed. The source code for the numerical simulations is available at https://github.com/astrophysics/mean-field-dynamo. Molecular eruptions are hypothesized to be a primary mechanism for the rapid formation of massive stars. This study presents ALMA observations of a molecular eruption occurring in the circumnuclear region of the nearby starburst galaxy NGC 4945. The eruption is characterized by a dense, compact molecular core with a mass of approximately 100 solar masses and a radius of roughly 0.1 parsecs, which is expanding at a velocity of about 10 km/s. This study introduces a conservative finite element approach for quasilinear diffusion equations, which are essential for modeling the evolution of distribution functions in magnetized plasmas. The method employs a finite element discretization of the Fokker-Planck operator, utilizing a Galerkin formulation with a specific choice of test functions to ensure the conservation of particle number. This technique is applied to the Landau operator, a quasilinear diffusion framework widely used in plasma physics. The proposed scheme is validated through two test cases: the diffusion of a Maxwellian distribution and the relaxation of a bi-Maxwellian distribution toward a Maxwellian state. The results demonstrate that the method accurately preserves the total particle number and achieves the expected relaxation dynamics. Furthermore, the method's applicability extends to other quasilinear diffusion operators, such as the Rosenbluth operator, which governs diffusion in unmagnetized plasmas. The code implementing this approach is publicly accessible at https://github.com/andrewjgibson/conservative-fem. The source code is also included in the supplementary material. We present a new method for identifying the intergalactic medium (IGM) surrounding dwarf galaxies, utilizing the spatial distribution of ionized gas detected via H$\alpha$ emission. This approach is applied to the dwarf irregular galaxy NGC 6822, revealing an extended H$\alpha$-emitting region that reaches approximately 1.5 kpc beyond the galaxy's visible edge. We estimate the total mass of this ionized gas to be roughly $10^5$ M$_\odot$, with a density of about $10^{-4}$ cm$^{-3}$ and a temperature near 10,000 K. These characteristics align with those of the warm ionized medium found in the IGM of other dwarf galaxies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the ionized gas within NGC 6822 is in a state of hydrostatic equilibrium, suggesting that the IGM of dwarf galaxies is not merely a passive byproduct of galactic evolution but may play an active role in shaping their histories. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the broader understanding of the IGM. Furthermore, we observe that the quasiparticle weight of bosons remains finite at this critical coupling. These results offer valuable insights into the quasiparticle characteristics of fermions interacting with local bosons. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the quasiparticle properties of fermions coupled to bosonic baths. This paper investigates the divergence properties of the braided Thompson groups $VB_n$ and $VW_n$, as well as the generalized Thompson groups $G_n$ and $GW_n$. We establish that for any $n \geq 2$, the divergence of $VB_n$ and $VW_n$ is precisely $n$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the divergence of $G_n$ and $GW_n$ is bounded by $n$ and $n+1$, respectively. Additionally, we prove that the divergence of $G_n$ is unbounded as $n$ increases. Finally, we provide a characterization of the divergence for $GW_n$ by examining the action of these groups on the simplicial tree $T_n$. These findings extend earlier results regarding the divergence of the classical Thompson group $F$ and the braided Thompson group $VF$. This study examines a directed hybrid random graph model that integrates the preferential attachment mechanism with uniform linkage rules. In this framework, a new vertex connects to an existing one with a probability proportional to the latter's out-degree, while the remaining connection probability is distributed uniformly across all other vertices. We demonstrate that the out-degree distribution of this hybrid model converges to a power law with an exponent of 3, provided the initial out-degree distribution is sufficiently heavy-tailed. Furthermore, we establish that the in-degree distribution also follows a power law, with an exponent that depends on the specific parameters of the model. Finally, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of the diameter and the average path length within this hybrid random graph. The primary methodology employed involves the analysis of generating functions. Additionally, we provide a numerical simulation to validate our theoretical findings. The code used for these simulations is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/DirHybRandGraph. This study introduces a multi-label wireless disturbance detection system utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). The CNN is trained on a dataset of 1,000 labeled images depicting various wireless disturbances, including those caused by human hands, fingers, and other objects. The system's performance is evaluated using metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Experimental results indicate that the proposed system achieves a 99.9% accuracy rate. Furthermore, the system demonstrates the ability to identify multiple disturbances occurring simultaneously. We introduce a new exclusive observable, the proton recoil polarization, which is sensitive to the Gerasimov-Drell-Hiagen (GDH) integral. This quantity is expected to be non-zero in the photoproduction region and to vanish at the elastic point. We outline the experimental requirements needed to measure this observable and discuss its potential for probing the spin structure of the nucleon. Furthermore, we present a preliminary analysis of the proton polarization in the elastic regime, incorporating both leading-order perturbative QCD calculations and a model based on the proton's constituent quarks. Our results indicate that the proton polarization is non-zero and exhibits a distinct dependence on the photon virtuality. Finally, we highlight the significance of this observable for future experiments at the Electron-Ion Collider. We present a theoretical analysis of the thermal shift in the modulation-driven superfluid transition for bosons with spin-orbit coupling within an optical lattice. Our findings indicate that the thermal shift is highly sensitive to the specific spin-orbit coupling mechanism. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the shift can be effectively suppressed by adjusting the modulation frequency. Finally, we outline a potential experimental approach to realize this system using ultracold atoms. These results offer a pathway to investigate the thermal behavior of spin-orbit coupled superfluids and may enable the creation of novel quantum materials. Additionally, the methodology developed here is applicable to other periodically driven quantum systems. We investigate novel findings in reduced AdS/CFT by analyzing the corresponding bulk theory. Specifically, we examine the dimensional reduction of Type IIA supergravity on a circle, focusing on the AdS$_4$/CFT$_3$ duality. We demonstrate that the bulk theory retains a significant number of fields, including those associated with the Kaluza-Klein vector, which are essential for the duality. Furthermore, we show that the Kaluza-Klein vector field in the bulk corresponds to the R-symmetry current in the boundary CFT. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the holographic duality. Additionally, we explore the dimensional reduction of Type IIA supergravity on a two-sphere, which yields a five-dimensional bulk theory. We argue that this reduced theory is also viable for the AdS$_4$/CFT$_3$ duality. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the holographic duality. Beam-induced background radiation is a critical factor in the design of muon colliders, as it can generate noise that interferes with the detection of physics signals. This study examines various strategies to mitigate such beam-induced noise at muon colliders. We demonstrate that the noise level can be substantially reduced by strategically selecting the interaction point and by employing a beam with a large crossing angle. Furthermore, we show that the impact of beam-induced noise on the muon collider's physics potential can be effectively minimized through the implementation of these mitigation techniques. Finally, we outline the necessary steps to incorporate beam-induced noise into the design of a muon collider. These findings are applicable to both circular and linear collider configurations. We introduce Spartan, a new framework for training sparse neural networks that utilizes a differentiable approximation of the regularized optimal transport problem. Spartan offers a straightforward and efficient approach to sparse training, enabling the creation of sparse models with minimal modifications to existing architectures. We demonstrate that Spartan can be integrated into various sparse training methods, including magnitude pruning, lottery tickets, and magnitude-based regularization. Furthermore, we show that Spartan can be applied to both structured and unstructured sparsity. Our results indicate that Spartan achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and GLUE. We demonstrate that a weakly interacting Bose fluid confined to two dimensions exhibits an emergent Pauli obstruction, preventing the occupation of the lowest Landau level. This phenomenon arises from the competition between the bosonic exclusion principle and the repulsive interactions within the fluid. Our findings are validated through both variational Monte Carlo simulations and exact diagonalization of the system's Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we show that this emergent Pauli blocking can be utilized to construct a robust, strongly correlated quantum fluid. These results offer a novel method for generating exotic quantum states of matter and provide a new perspective on the fundamental characteristics of bosonic fluids. Additionally, we suggest that this effect may be observable in ultracold atomic gases. Finally, we explore the broader implications of our findings for the study of strongly correlated quantum fluids. The source code used for the variational Monte Carlo simulations is available at https://github.com/robertkennedy1992/bose-obstruction. This paper introduces KKMCee, a Monte Carlo event generator designed for lepton colliders that simulates the production of lepton and quark pairs. The program calculates the cross section for the process $e^+e^- \to \gamma^*/Z^* \to f\bar{f}$, where $f$ represents any fermion pair, incorporating initial-state radiation, final-state QED and QCD corrections, and the interference between photon and $Z$-boson exchange. It also accounts for the interference between the $\gamma^*/Z^*$ and the Higgs boson in the process $e^+e^- \to \gamma^*/Z^* \to f\bar{f}h$. This study introduces a novel approach to Inter-Beat Interval (IBI) estimation, utilizing the Tiramisu framework to enhance the accuracy of the widely used Photoplethysmogram (PPG) signal. The method involves three primary stages: (1) denoising the PPG signal using the Tiramisu framework, (2) detecting peaks within the denoised signal, and (3) calculating the IBI from the identified peaks. The proposed technique was evaluated using the PPGDB1 dataset, which comprises 100 PPG signals from 10 subjects. Results indicate that the proposed method achieves a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.01 seconds, representing a 50% reduction in error compared to the standard peak detection method. Additionally, the method demonstrates robustness against motion artifacts, maintaining an MAE of 0.01 seconds even when signals are corrupted by these disturbances. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/IBI-estimation. The findings confirm that the proposed method is effective for IBI estimation and holds significant potential for future research. Furthermore, the method is highly adaptable, allowing for the integration of various denoising techniques to further improve IBI estimation accuracy. The authors believe this approach will be valuable for advancing research in the field. This study introduces a stochastic algorithm for tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) that utilizes an unrestricted number of passes. The method is grounded in a stochastic gradient descent approach, which iteratively refines the initial estimate of the tensor singular subspace. We demonstrate that this iterative process converges to the true singular subspace with high probability. Furthermore, we establish that the algorithm achieves linear convergence in expectation, provided the initial estimate is sufficiently close to the target subspace. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to validate the algorithm's efficacy. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/TSVD.

Graphs are fundamental to modeling numerous real-world systems, and graph embeddings have become a widely adopted technique for representing these structures. However, most existing embedding methods are designed for static graphs, whereas many real-world networks are dynamic and evolve over time. This paper investigates the challenge of embedding evolving graphs. We begin by reviewing current approaches for dynamic graphs and identifying their limitations. Subsequently, we examine the specific requirements for embedding evolving graphs and analyze the trade-offs between different methods. Finally, we outline several open research questions in this domain. Our goal is to provide a comprehensive overview of graph embedding for evolving graphs and to inspire further research in this area. We introduce a novel framework for learning optimal representations of data within a deep neural network. This approach employs a deep autoencoder to map data into a latent space, where a deep auto-regularizer is applied to the latent representations. The auto-regularizer is defined as the Sinkhorn distance between the data distribution and a reference distribution, which is derived from a set of labeled data. We demonstrate that the gradients of this auto-regularizer can be efficiently computed using a single forward and backward pass through the autoencoder. Furthermore, we establish that the proposed method is equivalent to a specific form of adversarial training. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets indicate that our method yields superior representations compared to existing techniques. Additionally, we show that these learned representations enhance the performance of various downstream classifiers. Finally, we provide theoretical insights into the properties of the learned representations. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1995/SinkhornAutoRegularizer. Contact tracing is a vital strategy for curbing the spread of COVID-19, yet its efficacy relies heavily on the speed of case identification and contact notification. While tracing is most effective when implemented nationally, regional variations in testing and tracing capabilities can create disparities in case detection and notification rates. This study evaluates how such differences impact the overall effectiveness of contact tracing. We developed a stochastic, agent-based model of COVID-19 transmission within England, incorporating regional variations in testing and tracing. Our findings indicate that regional disparities in case detection and contact notification can significantly alter the transmission dynamics of COVID-19. Furthermore, we observed that the effectiveness of contact tracing is highly sensitive to the proportion of cases identified and the speed of contact notification. Finally, we demonstrated that regional collaborations in tracing can substantially enhance the performance of contact tracing programs. These results underscore the necessity for a unified, national contact tracing system to ensure the strategy's success. Additionally, they highlight the critical importance of rapid case detection and swift contact notification, suggesting that future efforts should prioritize improving these specific aspects. Our primary finding demonstrates that, for a fixed dimension $d$, the $i$-th Betti number of an RSC converges in distribution to a Poisson random variable with parameter $\lambda_i(c)$ as $N$ approaches infinity. Furthermore, we establish that $\lambda_i(c)$ remains finite for all $c > 0$ and $i \geq 0$ when $d=2$, and for $c > 0$ and $i \geq 1$ when $d \geq 3$. In contrast, we show that $\lambda_i(c)$ diverges to infinity for $i \geq 0$ when $d \geq 3$ and $c$ exceeds a specific threshold $c_i$. Additionally, we derive the asymptotic behavior of $\lambda_i(c)$ as $c$ tends to infinity for $d=2$ and $i \geq 0$, as well as for $d \geq 3$ and $i \geq 1$. Finally, we present a conjecture regarding the asymptotic behavior of $\lambda_i(c)$ for $d \geq 3$ and $i \geq 1$ in the limit where $c$ approaches zero. These results are derived through a novel analysis of the sparse domain, which relies on the theory of random graphs and the sparse limit of simplicial complexes. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) aims to derive a reward function from expert demonstrations. This paper introduces a novel approach called inverse restricted reinforcement learning (IRRL), which incorporates prior knowledge about the reward function into the IRL framework. We present two distinct methods for formulating IRRL as a convex optimization problem. The first method employs a linear programming formulation, while the second utilizes a quadratic programming approach. We provide theoretical analysis of the conditions under which IRRL yields a unique solution and demonstrate its application to a simple grid-world scenario. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of IRRL against standard IRL techniques using both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results indicate that IRRL surpasses traditional IRL methods when prior information regarding the reward function is available. We introduce a new vertex divider that partitions a graph into two components with bounded treewidth, where the size of the separator is also bounded. This divider is constructed using a space-efficient algorithm that operates within logarithmic space. Our approach yields a space-efficient treewidth decomposition algorithm for graphs with bounded genus, achieving a logarithmic space complexity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method can be applied to graph problems solvable via treewidth-based algorithms, such as finding maximum independent sets and determining graph coloring. Consequently, we establish that these problems can be solved within logarithmic space. Finally, we extend our results to graphs with bounded treewidth, proving that the maximum independent set problem can be solved in logarithmic space. Additionally, we show that the treewidth of a graph can be computed in logarithmic space. These findings are achieved by developing a novel, space-efficient algorithm for vertex dividers that relies on the graph's treewidth decomposition. Our results are particularly significant for graphs with genus $g$, as they establish a treewidth bound of $O(g \log g)$, which is nearly optimal. This optimal bound was previously established by Thomassen (1989) and Mohar (1988). We also provide a space-efficient algorithm for vertex dividers that runs in polynomial time. This algorithm is derived from a new, space-efficient algorithm for treewidth decomposition, which is based on the Baker's layering technique. The resulting polynomial-time algorithm for vertex dividers is the first of its kind to achieve a separator size of $O(\sqrt{g})$. Grouping algorithms are essential for analyzing complex networks, yet their application to directed networks remains underexplored. This study examines the theoretical foundations of grouping within directed networks, specifically focusing on weighted directed grouping. We demonstrate that the standard clustering coefficient, a key metric in undirected networks, lacks a direct equivalent in directed contexts. Furthermore, we establish that weighted directed grouping is fundamentally distinct from weighted undirected grouping, as the latter cannot be derived from the former. Consequently, we propose a novel algorithm for weighted directed grouping and provide a comprehensive analysis of its properties. Finally, we illustrate the algorithm's utility by applying it to a network of inferred gene regulatory interactions. Our results indicate that the algorithm successfully identifies biologically relevant groups, including those corresponding to known transcription factor families. These findings underscore the necessity of developing and utilizing appropriate grouping methods for directed networks. Additionally, we argue that grouping algorithms should be evaluated using both synthetic and real-world data, as well as through rigorous theoretical analysis. We contend that such evaluations are critical for advancing the field of network analysis. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are a recent machine learning approach designed to solve partial differential equations (PDEs) by integrating physical laws into the learning process. This paper introduces a novel method for evaluating PINN solutions that does not rely on the training data. The approach involves training a second neural network to identify the most probable solution to the PDE, which is then compared against the PINN output. This technique is demonstrated on a simple PDE and a complex, high-dimensional system of PDEs. The results indicate that the proposed method can detect errors in PINN solutions, even in scenarios where the PINN appears to have converged. Furthermore, the method is capable of identifying the specific source of these errors. Finally, the study explores the potential of this approach for enhancing PINN performance. Atmospheric pollution is a significant contributor to global morbidity and mortality. This study introduces a novel methodology for modeling atmospheric contamination, integrating geostatistics and artificial intelligence to analyze the relationship between air quality and epidemiological data. The approach involves two primary stages: first, estimating the spatial distribution of pollutants using geostatistical techniques, and second, analyzing the correlation between these estimated concentrations and epidemiological outcomes via artificial intelligence. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through a case study examining the impact of air pollution on respiratory health. Results indicate that the proposed approach yields promising outcomes, offering a robust framework for future research in this domain. We introduce a method to distinguish the Majorana peak from other peaks in tunneling spectroscopy, accounting for Ohmic dissipation. This approach involves measuring the differential conductance of a Majorana mode using both metallic and dielectric resistive electrodes. The resulting conductance spectra for each electrode type exhibit distinct characteristics, enabling the differentiation of the Majorana peak. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dielectric resistive electrode is highly effective for observing the Majorana peak, even in scenarios where Ohmic dissipation is significant. This study provides a novel experimental strategy for identifying Majorana modes. Additionally, we show that the dielectric resistive electrode can be realized through a simple modification of the tunneling setup. Finally, we discuss the potential for observing the Majorana peak in a realistic environment where Ohmic dissipation is unavoidable. These findings offer a new perspective for investigating Majorana modes. Our proposed experimental method is applicable to various systems hosting Majorana modes, including those based on topological superconductors and those involving Majorana fermions in quantum Hall states. We believe this work will inspire further experimental research into Majorana modes. The source code for the simulations is available at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/Ohmic_dissipation. This study examines the online learning problem within linear bandits featuring diverse action sets, where the objective is to minimize cumulative regret. We introduce a novel algorithm that achieves a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$, matching the performance of standard linear bandit algorithms with homogeneous action sets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this algorithm is optimal up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we explore the implications of this framework for statistical inference, specifically addressing the challenge of constructing confidence intervals for the mean reward of a new action. We propose a method to build such intervals for unseen actions and prove that it is optimal up to logarithmic factors. Additionally, we show that this approach is equivalent to a recently introduced method for linear regression with covariates outside the design matrix. Our findings are supported by both theoretical analysis and numerical experiments. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robin-berthier/linear_bandits_diverse_action_sets.

Keywords: Linear bandits, diverse action sets, inference, confidence intervals.

This paper introduces a new navigation framework designed for self-governing robots, termed Profound Active Deduction (PAD). The system's core objective is to enable robots to navigate autonomously by actively deducing their current location and the positions of landmarks within a map. PAD integrates a novel active deduction algorithm with a new landmark recognition method. The algorithm utilizes a new representation of the robot's belief state, which is updated through a combination of active deduction and belief revision. Furthermore, the landmark recognition method employs a new feature extraction technique to identify landmarks based on the robot's belief state. Experimental results demonstrate that PAD successfully navigates a robot through a maze and a real-world environment, effectively handling noisy sensor data and landmark occlusions. Additionally, the system exhibits robustness against errors in the robot's initial belief state. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. Automated Composition Evaluation (ACE) involves assessing the quality of student essays using various metrics. While prior research has primarily focused on evaluating essay quality through Transformer-based language models, this study introduces a novel approach that leverages the model's ability to generate text. By employing a text generation model, we can assess the quality of an essay by comparing it against a reference essay. We present a new metric, the Effective Text Generation (ETG) score, which measures the similarity between two essays by calculating the probability that a model generates one essay given the other. We also introduce a new dataset, the Common European Proficiency Scale (CEPS) dataset, comprising essays from the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) exams. Our experimental results demonstrate that the ETG score effectively correlates with human evaluations of essay quality. Furthermore, we show that the ETG score surpasses other existing metrics in predicting essay quality. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the ETG score's performance across different model sizes and configurations. Domain adaptation is a prevalent strategy for enhancing pedestrian identification performance in unconstrained environments. However, existing domain adaptive methods often suffer from false positives, where individuals from the target domain are incorrectly matched to a query image. To address this, we introduce a novel approach called Box Reordering, which leverages the inherent ordering of bounding boxes to filter out these false positives. This method is unsupervised, requiring no additional annotations, and is compatible with any domain adaptive pedestrian identification model. Extensive experiments on the challenging cross-domain dataset MARS demonstrate that our approach significantly reduces false positives while maintaining high recall rates. Throwing is a fundamental human action that is essential for daily life and critical in sports. While prior research has extensively examined the biomechanics of throwing, it has largely overlooked the effects of errors in the point of release. This study aims to investigate how incorrect release points influence throwing performance. To achieve this, we developed a new simulation framework called FauxThrow, which models the human throwing process by integrating a musculoskeletal model with a physics-based throwing model. We conducted a series of experiments to analyze the impact of release point errors on throwing outcomes. The results indicate that errors in the release point significantly affect throwing performance, with the magnitude of these effects varying based on the direction of the error. Furthermore, we observed that the body's compensatory mechanisms for release point errors differ depending on the error's direction. These findings offer valuable insights for designing training programs to enhance throwing skills and for developing rehabilitation strategies for individuals with throwing injuries. Additionally, the FauxThrow framework can be utilized to investigate other factors influencing throwing performance. We introduce a new method for estimating the projector fidelity of quantum states, a metric that quantifies how closely a state aligns with a specific target subspace. This approach utilizes shallow random Clifford circuits to generate a set of random states, which are then measured against the target subspace projector. The resulting fidelity estimate is derived from the average of these individual measurements. We demonstrate that this technique achieves a constant-depth complexity, offering a significant advantage over existing methods. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the method's statistical properties, including its bias, variance, and convergence rate. Finally, we validate the approach through numerical simulations and experimental data obtained from the IBM quantum computer. Our results indicate that the method is both accurate and efficient, making it a valuable tool for characterizing quantum states and subspaces. This work holds particular significance for near-term quantum devices, where state preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors are prevalent. By enabling the estimation of projector fidelity despite these errors, our method facilitates the evaluation of quantum algorithms and protocols, thereby aiding in the development of more robust and reliable quantum software. Ultimately, this research contributes to the advancement of quantum computing and the realization of practical quantum applications. Automatic vertebra recognition and positioning are critical for numerous clinical tasks, including vertebra segmentation, spine deformity analysis, and surgical planning. However, the complex anatomy of the spine and the presence of artifacts in CT images often hinder the performance of deep learning models. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel spine rectification method that utilizes a lightweight deep learning model to automatically correct spine deformations. Additionally, we propose an anatomically-constrained enhancement approach that leverages the known anatomical structure of the spine to improve the accuracy of vertebra recognition. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively rectifies spine deformations and significantly enhances vertebra recognition performance. We investigate the resonant scattering of electrons by a standing wave of light within a cavity, focusing on the regime of extremely strong coupling. In this context, the electron's wave function is dynamically stabilized against ionization through vacuum oscillations between dressed states. This stabilization mechanism is analyzed using both a perturbative approach and a non-perturbative method based on the Floquet formalism. Our findings indicate that the resonant scattering cross section exhibits a dependence on the light intensity that differs from the perturbative predictions. Furthermore, we observe that the electron wave function becomes localized in the region of highest field intensity, a phenomenon that can be interpreted as a form of dynamical localization. Finally, we demonstrate that the electron's energy is shifted by a value proportional to the square of the light intensity. These results are derived for a simplified model of an electron interacting with a standing wave, but they are expected to hold for more complex scenarios involving multi-electron atoms and molecules. The proposed experimental setup offers a means to probe the strong-field regime of light-matter interaction, which is currently beyond the reach of existing experiments. Additionally, this work provides a theoretical foundation for the development of new light sources, such as electron-driven free-electron lasers. The study of resonant scattering in the strong-field regime is also anticipated to yield insights into the fundamental nature of light-matter interactions. We introduce a variational approach to the quantum divisibility problem, which seeks to determine whether a quantum channel can be expressed as a convex combination of unital channels. This method is demonstrated on a family of non-unital qubit channels, revealing a phase transition between divisible and non-divisible regimes. Furthermore, we establish that the variational distance between the channel and the set of unital channels serves as a tight upper bound for the channel's non-unitality. Finally, we propose a conjecture regarding the convexity of this variational distance. These findings offer a novel perspective on the quantum divisibility problem and provide a practical framework for investigating the non-unitality of quantum channels. Additionally, our results may have applications in quantum thermodynamics, particularly concerning the non-unitality of thermalizing channels. This study examines the linear stability of a collisionless tearing mode within a slab plasma, where the current sheet is thin and the ion Larmor radius is comparable to the sheet's half-width. The analysis reveals that the mode is unstable, with the growth rate scaling as $\gamma \sim \omega_{*e} \delta^{3/2} \lambda_i^{1/2}$. Furthermore, the mode is found to be highly sensitive to the electron temperature gradient. Finally, the characteristics of the mode are compared against those of a large-scale tearing mode. The results indicate that the mini-scale tearing mode is significantly more unstable than its large-scale counterpart, a finding that aligns with recent experimental observations. Additionally, the study addresses the nonlinear evolution of the mode, demonstrating that it develops into a helical structure with a wavelength of $\lambda \sim \lambda_i$. This evolution is driven by the generation of a magnetic field component along the current sheet, which arises from the $\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}$ force. The resulting helical structure is identified as a magnetic island. Finally, the characteristics of this magnetic island are compared with those of a large-scale tearing mode. The findings suggest that the magnetic island associated with the mini-scale tearing mode is much smaller than that of the large-scale mode, a conclusion that is consistent with experimental data. These results are expected to be applicable to the study of edge localized modes in tokamak plasmas. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these findings. Fashion image retrieval involves identifying images sharing a specific attribute, such as color, style, or pattern. While recent methods have achieved notable success, they often depend on extensive datasets and are limited to handling only a few attributes. This paper introduces a semi-supervised approach that learns a feature representation capable of encoding multiple attributes, thereby enabling the manipulation of numerous traits. The method utilizes a multi-task learning framework to train a shared feature extractor alongside multiple attribute classifiers. To ensure the learned representation is both discriminative and semantically meaningful, the approach incorporates a novel loss function that enforces orthogonality among attribute representations. Furthermore, a feature-level manipulation technique is developed to alter the attributes of a given image within this learned space. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in both retrieval accuracy and the ability to manipulate multiple attributes. This paper introduces a dual gradient ascent approach to tackle linear ill-posed problems within Banach spaces. The proposed method is demonstrated to converge to the minimum norm solution of the associated dual problem. Furthermore, numerical experiments are conducted to validate the theoretical findings. Finally, the study examines the application of this method to the linearized inverse conductivity problem. The results indicate that the dual gradient ascent method achieves superior reconstruction quality compared to the truncated singular value decomposition (TSVD) method. Additionally, the method exhibits robustness against noise, as evidenced by its ability to produce high-quality reconstructions even when the data is corrupted by noise at a level of 10%. These numerical findings are consistent with the theoretical analysis. Consequently, the dual gradient ascent method is recommended for solving linear ill-posed problems in Banach spaces. This paper introduces a novel approach for selecting Access Points (APs) and Extenders (EXTs) within IEEE 802.11 networks, designed to minimize interference and optimize throughput. The proposed method leverages IEEE 802.11k/v standards to gather channel load data from neighboring APs and EXTs, enabling the system to identify the optimal AP/EXT for a mobile station. By utilizing this channel load information, the system can dynamically adjust the transmit power of the chosen AP/EXT to further reduce interference. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed scheme significantly lowers interference and enhances throughput compared to existing solutions. Additionally, the method exhibits robustness against inaccuracies in channel load measurements. The study also addresses the challenges of implementing this scheme in real-world environments, specifically focusing on the reliability of channel load data and the impact of measurement errors. Finally, the paper outlines the necessary modifications to the IEEE 802.11 standard to support this proposed solution. The authors intend to implement this scheme in a real-world setting to validate its effectiveness.
